title: What is light? Energy that spreads out, warms things and has a family you cannot see

summary.text: A tar road is too hot to walk on at noon, while a whitewashed wall beside it stays much cooler, yet the same sunlight falls on both. A lamp across the street looks dim, although the lamp has not changed at all. A TV remote sends out light that your eyes cannot see, but a phone camera can. In this unit your child measures how a torch beam thins out as it travels, races ice cubes on black and white paper, and finds the invisible light of a remote control. They learn that light is energy, that it spreads out and turns into heat when a surface takes it in, and that the light we see is one thin slice of a long family of waves.
summary.art: A tar road and a whitewashed wall side by side in strong sunshine, a phone held up to a TV remote showing a purple glow, and a small lamp far down the street looking dim.

intro.hook: Imagine standing barefoot on a tar road at noon (do not try it, it can burn), then stepping into the cool shade of a whitewashed wall. Same Sun, same sunlight. Why is the road so hot? Where did the light go when it landed on the road?
intro.text: Light does not just let us see. It carries energy, and when a surface takes the light in, that energy turns into heat. A lamp far away looks dim for a different reason. Its light spreads out over a wider and wider space, so each patch of your eye gets less. In this unit you will measure how fast a torch beam thins out, race ice cubes on black paper and white paper, and use a phone camera to catch light your eyes cannot see. You will also meet the long family of waves that light belongs to, from radio to X-rays.
intro.art: A child in a dark room holding a torch toward squared paper on a wall, with the beam shown widening like a cone, and a bar of coloured light at the side labelled the family of light.

outcomes: I can explain that light is energy, and that the same light gets thinner as it spreads out in all directions.
I can show with a torch and squared paper that going twice as far makes the light cover four times the area.
I can explain that a surface takes in light and turns it into heat, and why a dark surface warms faster than a white one.
I can name the members of the light family, from radio waves to gamma rays, and say they are the same kind of wave with different wavelengths.
I can find the invisible infrared light of a TV remote with a phone camera, and say what that shows about the limits of my eyes.
I can explain that light carries a tiny push, and how that push bends the tails of comets and could drive a solar sail.
I can follow the energy in my food back to the Sun.
I can tell how William Herschel found invisible light in 1800, and say what scientists agree on and what is still not known.

terms.meaning: Light is energy that travels in straight lines from a source and lets us see. Some of it can warm things up.
terms.example: Sunlight warms a steel tumbler left on a windowsill.
terms.art: Sunbeams falling through a window onto a steel tumbler on a sill.

terms.meaning: Energy is what makes things happen. It can move things, warm things and light things up. It is never used up. It only changes from one kind to another.
terms.example: A lit diya turns the energy stored in oil into light and heat.
terms.art: A small lit oil lamp with arrows labelled light and heat leaving it.

terms.meaning: To spread out means to cover a bigger and bigger space as you go further from the start. Light from a lamp spreads out in all directions.
terms.example: A drop of ink on wet blotting paper spreads out in a circle that keeps growing.
terms.art: A torch beam shown as a cone, growing wider from the torch to a wall.

terms.meaning: Brightness is how much light lands on a patch of a surface, or on your eye. A patch that gets more light looks brighter.
terms.example: A page near a lamp is brighter than the same page at the far end of the room.
terms.art: Two pages, one near a lamp and glowing, one far from it and dim.

terms.meaning: To absorb light is to take it in instead of sending it back. The light's energy turns into heat inside the thing.
terms.example: A black umbrella absorbs most of the sunlight that falls on it, so the cloth gets warm.
terms.art: A black umbrella in sunshine with arrows going in and small wavy lines of heat rising.

terms.meaning: To reflect light is to bounce it back instead of taking it in. A surface that reflects most light stays cooler.
terms.example: A white wall reflects most sunlight, which is why white walls feel cooler.
terms.art: A white wall with sunbeams arriving and bouncing off again.

terms.meaning: Heat is energy that moves from a warmer thing to a cooler thing, and makes the cooler thing warmer. It is the jiggling of the tiny particles inside a thing.
terms.example: Heat flows from a hot tumbler of tea into your cold hands.
terms.art: A steaming steel tumbler with arrows going into two cupped hands.

terms.meaning: Visible light is the kind of light our eyes can see. It runs from violet to red, the colours of a rainbow.
terms.example: The coloured band that a glass of water throws on a wall is made of visible light.
terms.art: A rainbow band with violet at one end and red at the other.

terms.meaning: Infrared is light that is just beyond red. Our eyes cannot see it, but our skin feels it as warmth. Every warm thing gives it out.
terms.example: A TV remote sends an infrared signal to the TV.
terms.art: A TV remote with dotted lines going to a TV, drawn in a pale red.

terms.meaning: Ultraviolet is light that is just beyond violet. Our eyes cannot see it. It carries more energy than visible light and can burn skin.
terms.example: Sunburn on a long day at the beach comes from ultraviolet light.
terms.art: A child on a beach with a hat and a faint violet wash over the sand.

terms.meaning: Radio waves are the longest waves in the light family. Our eyes cannot see them. They carry radio, TV and phone signals.
terms.example: The song on an FM radio reaches you on radio waves about 3 metres long.
terms.art: A radio tower with long, wide waves spreading from it to a small radio on a table.

terms.meaning: Microwaves are waves a little shorter than radio waves. They carry Wi-Fi and phone signals, and they heat food in a microwave oven.
terms.example: A Wi-Fi router sends microwaves about 12 centimetres long through your home.
terms.art: A Wi-Fi router in a living room with short waves reaching a phone and a laptop.

terms.meaning: X-rays are waves much shorter than visible light. They carry a lot of energy. They pass through soft parts of the body but are stopped by bone.
terms.example: A hospital X-ray photo shows the bones of a broken arm.
terms.art: An X-ray picture of a hand with the bones glowing white.

terms.meaning: Gamma rays are the shortest waves in the light family and carry the most energy. They come from exploding stars and from some atoms.
terms.example: Doctors use carefully aimed gamma rays to treat some cancers.
terms.art: A star exploding in space with short, sharp waves spreading out.

terms.meaning: Wavelength is the distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next. The members of the light family differ in wavelength.
terms.example: The wavelength of red light is about 100 times smaller than the width of a hair.
terms.art: A wavy line with two neighbouring tops marked and the gap between them labelled wavelength.

terms.meaning: The electromagnetic spectrum is the whole family of light waves, lined up from the longest wavelength to the shortest. Visible light is one small part of it.
terms.example: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all in the electromagnetic spectrum.
terms.art: A long coloured ribbon with radio at one end and gamma rays at the other, and a tiny rainbow in the middle.

terms.meaning: A prism is a block of clear glass or plastic, often shaped like a triangle. It splits white light into a band of colours.
terms.example: Sunlight through a glass prism makes a rainbow on the wall.
terms.art: A triangle of glass splitting a white beam into a rainbow band.

terms.meaning: A thermometer is a tool that measures how hot or cold something is. Most have a thin tube with liquid that rises when it gets warmer.
terms.example: A doctor puts a thermometer under your arm to check for fever.
terms.art: A glass thermometer with a red line rising along a scale.

terms.meaning: A control in a test is a thing you leave alone, so you can compare it with the things you changed. It shows what happens when nothing special is done.
terms.example: In the ice test, one ice cube sits on a plain plate as the control.
terms.art: Three ice cubes on three plates, one plain plate marked control.

terms.meaning: Radiation pressure is the tiny push that light gives to anything it lands on. It is very weak, but it is real.
terms.example: Sunlight pushes on a spacecraft, with a force about the weight of a grain of sugar on each square metre.
terms.art: A shiny spacecraft sail with tiny arrows of sunlight pushing on it.

terms.meaning: A solar sail is a huge, thin, shiny sheet on a spacecraft. Sunlight pushes it, so the spacecraft needs no fuel.
terms.example: A Japanese spacecraft called IKAROS unfolded a solar sail in space in 2010.
terms.art: A small spacecraft with a big square shiny sail, with sunlight arrows pushing it.

terms.meaning: A comet is a ball of ice and dust that goes round the Sun. When it gets near the Sun, it grows a glowing tail that points away from the Sun.
terms.example: A comet's tail can be millions of kilometres long.
terms.art: A comet with a bright head and a long tail pointing away from a distant Sun.

terms.meaning: Photosynthesis is how plants use sunlight to make food from air and water. The energy of the light is stored in the food.
terms.example: A rice plant in a paddy field uses photosynthesis to make the grains you eat.
terms.art: A green leaf with sunlight arriving, and water and air going in, and sugar coming out.

explanations.concept: Light is energy on the move
explanations.definition: Light is a kind of energy that travels. When it lands on something, it can warm it, make a chemical change in it, or push electrons around in it.
explanations.description: Light leaves a lamp, a fire or the Sun and carries energy away with it. That energy does not vanish when the light lands. It turns into something else. Sunlight on a steel tumbler turns into heat. Sunlight on a leaf turns into the stored energy of sugar. Sunlight on a solar panel pushes electrons along a wire and makes electricity. In every case, the light is gone and the same amount of energy is still there, in a new form.
examples: A solar water heater on a roof in Chennai turns sunlight into hot water for a whole family.
A leaf turns sunlight into sugar, which the plant uses to grow.
A solar calculator keeps working with no battery as long as light falls on its small panel.
explanations.art: Sunlight arriving at three places, a steel tumbler, a leaf and a solar panel, each with an arrow to heat, sugar and electricity.

explanations.concept: Light spreads out and gets thinner
explanations.definition: Light from a small source spreads out in all directions. Twice as far from the source, the same light covers four times the area, so each patch gets one quarter as much.
explanations.description: A torch sends its light out in a cone. Close to the torch, the cone is narrow and the light is packed tight. Further away, the cone is wider, and the same light is spread over a bigger patch. If you go twice as far, the patch is twice as wide and twice as tall. Two times two is four, so the patch is four times bigger. The same light is shared by four times the area, so each part of the patch is four times dimmer. At three times the distance, the area is nine times bigger and the light is nine times thinner. Scientists call this the inverse square law. Johannes Kepler wrote about it in the early 1600s.
examples: A lamp 2 metres away gives a page one quarter of the light it gives at 1 metre.
Jupiter is about 5 times further from the Sun than the Earth. Each square metre there gets about 25 times less sunlight.
A street light at the end of a long road looks dim, because its light has spread over a huge area by the time it reaches you.
explanations.art: A torch with a cone of light hitting squared paper at one, two and three torch-lengths away, with the lit patch covering 1, 4 and 9 squares.

explanations.concept: Dim does not mean used up
explanations.definition: In clear space, light is not used up as it travels. It only spreads over a bigger area, so each part of the area gets less.
explanations.description: Many people think light gets tired and weaker as it goes. In clear space, that is not what happens. Think of a bucket of water poured onto a floor. The same water makes a thick puddle if the floor is small and a thin film if the floor is huge. The amount of water has not changed. Light is like that. The total light going through a bigger and bigger sphere around a lamp stays the same. Only the light on each small patch gets less. Air with dust, smoke or fog does take in or scatter some light, so a lamp seen through fog looks dimmer still. Most of the dimming of a faraway star, however, is just spreading.
examples: A candle can be seen from a long way off on a dark night, because the light that reaches your eye is small but your eye still catches it.
Starlight crosses space for thousands of years and arrives with its energy intact. It is thin only because it has spread.
A street light looks dimmer in fog than on a clear night, because fog scatters some of its light away.
explanations.art: A lamp in the middle of two nested spheres, with the same four rays going through a small patch of the inner sphere and a bigger patch of the outer sphere.

explanations.concept: What a surface does with light: reflect, absorb or let it through
explanations.definition: When light lands on a surface, some is reflected, some is absorbed and some passes through. The three always add up to all of the light that arrived.
explanations.description: Think of three things that can happen to a cricket ball thrown at a wall, a net or an open door. It can bounce back, get caught, or go through. Light has the same three choices. A mirror reflects almost all of it. A black cloth absorbs almost all of it. Clear glass lets most of it through. Most things do a mix. White paper reflects most of the light but absorbs some. Thin paper reflects some, absorbs some and lets some through. What the surface is made of and how smooth it is decide the mix. For every surface, the three parts add up to all the light that landed.
examples: A polished steel plate reflects most of the light that lands on it.
Black cloth absorbs most of the light that lands on it.
A window pane lets most of the light through, and reflects and absorbs a little.
explanations.art: Three surfaces, a mirror, a black cloth and a window, each with a beam arriving and arrows showing the share reflected, absorbed and let through.

explanations.concept: When light is absorbed, it becomes heat
explanations.definition: When a surface absorbs light, the energy of the light turns into heat. The surface warms up.
explanations.description: Light that is absorbed is not lost. Its energy goes into the tiny particles that the surface is made of, and makes them jiggle faster. Faster jiggling is what we feel as heat. A black surface absorbs most of the sunlight that lands on it, so it warms up quickly. A white surface reflects most of it, so it warms up slowly. This is why people in hot places often wear white clothes and paint their roofs white, and why tar roads burn the soles of bare feet. A shiny sheet of aluminium foil reflects almost everything, so it stays cool even in the Sun. The energy is never lost. It changes from light to heat.
examples: A black plastic water tank on a roof gets hot much faster than a white one.
A tar road is far hotter than a whitewashed wall at noon.
A black umbrella warms the air under it more than a white one does.
explanations.art: A black tank and a white tank on a roof in strong sunshine, with arrows of sunlight going in on the black tank and bouncing off the white one.

explanations.concept: Where the Sun's light goes when it reaches the Earth
explanations.definition: The sunlight that reaches the Earth warms the land, sea and air, drives the weather and the water cycle, and is captured by plants, which feed almost all other life.
explanations.description: The Sun sends out light in every direction. The Earth catches only about one part in two billion of it. Even so, this is huge. The sunlight that falls on the Earth in one hour holds about as much energy as all of humanity uses in a year. Some of it warms the sea. The warm sea water evaporates, makes monsoon clouds and later falls as rain. Some of it warms the air unevenly and makes wind. A small part is caught by leaves and stored in food. The fuels we burn, such as coal, oil and gas, are the sunlight stored by plants and tiny sea creatures long ago.
examples: The south-west monsoon is driven by the Sun heating the land faster than the sea.
An idli is rice, and rice grew in sunlight. So the energy you use to run and think was sunlight, a short while ago.
Wind that turns the turbines in Tamil Nadu is air moved because the Sun heated some places more than others.
explanations.art: The Sun at the top, with arrows going down to the sea and clouds, a windmill, a rice field and a plate of idli.

explanations.concept: Light in, heat out: why the Earth stays at one temperature
explanations.definition: The Earth gives out as much infrared energy as it takes in as sunlight. The balance decides how warm the Earth is.
explanations.description: The Earth takes in sunlight all day. If nothing took the energy away, the Earth would keep getting hotter. But everything warm gives out infrared. The warm ground, sea and air send infrared back out into space. The Earth's temperature settles where the energy going out matches the energy coming in. Gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour catch some of the outgoing infrared and slow its escape. They act like a blanket. This is called the greenhouse effect. It keeps the Earth warm enough for life. Adding more carbon dioxide to the air makes the blanket thicker, so the Earth warms. Scientists across the world agree on this.
examples: A closed car left in the Sun gets very hot, because light gets in through the glass but the heat cannot escape easily.
Desert nights are cold, because the dry air holds little heat in. Cloudy nights are warmer, because clouds slow the escape of infrared.
The Moon has no air to act as a blanket, so its sunlit ground gets very hot and its night side gets very cold.
explanations.art: The Earth with yellow arrows of sunlight arriving and red wavy arrows of infrared leaving, with a thin layer of air catching some of them.

explanations.concept: One family of waves: the electromagnetic spectrum
explanations.definition: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same kind of wave. They differ only in wavelength.
explanations.description: Visible light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields. In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell worked out that such waves could be longer or shorter than light. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made the longer ones in a lab and showed they behave just like light. The whole family is called the electromagnetic spectrum. The members from longest to shortest are radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All of them travel at the speed of light in empty space. The shorter the wavelength, the more energy each photon carries. That is why a blue photon carries more than a red one, and an X-ray photon carries thousands of times more.
examples: FM radio waves are about 3 metres long. Wi-Fi waves are about 12 centimetres long.
Red light has a wavelength about 100 times smaller than the width of a hair.
X-rays can be as short as the width of an atom.
explanations.art: A long ribbon from radio waves at the left to gamma rays at the right, with wave drawings getting shorter and a tiny rainbow window in the middle.

explanations.concept: Radio waves and microwaves: the long waves that carry messages
explanations.definition: Radio waves and microwaves are the longest waves in the light family. They pass through walls and carry radio, TV, Wi-Fi and phone signals.
explanations.description: Long waves are not stopped by most walls, so they are good for sending messages. A radio station turns a voice or a song into a pattern of changes in radio waves. Your radio turns the pattern back into sound. Mobile phones and Wi-Fi use microwaves, a bit shorter. A microwave oven uses microwaves of the same family, but strong ones, to shake the water in food and warm it. Jagadish Chandra Bose, a scientist in Kolkata, showed around 1895 that waves a few millimetres long can pass through walls and ring a bell in another room. The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune uses 30 dishes to catch radio waves from far out in space.
examples: A phone call to a relative in Madurai travels as microwaves to a tower, then on through cables and more waves.
Radio telescopes found pulsars, which are spinning dead stars that blink many times a second.
Wi-Fi at home can get weaker as it passes through thick walls, because the walls absorb some of the waves.
explanations.art: A mobile phone tower with waves going to a house, and a row of big radio dishes under a night sky.

explanations.concept: Infrared: the warmth you can feel but not see
explanations.definition: Infrared is light just beyond red. Every warm thing gives it out, and our skin feels it as warmth.
explanations.description: The bigger the temperature of a thing, the more infrared it sends out. Your body gives out infrared, and so do a hot tava, a fire and a warm stone. You feel the heat of a fire on your face from a metre away because infrared from the fire lands on your skin. A thermal camera sees infrared and turns it into a coloured picture, so it can see warm bodies in the dark. Some snakes, such as pit vipers, have tiny pits on their faces that sense the infrared from a warm mouse. A TV remote uses infrared too. It sends a quick pattern of flickers, and the TV reads the pattern. The remote's light is invisible, but a phone camera can catch it.
examples: Sitting near a lit hearth, you feel its warmth long before you touch anything hot.
Thermal cameras at airports check whether travellers have a fever.
A pit viper senses a warm mouse in total darkness.
explanations.art: A thermal camera picture of a hand and a hot tumbler in orange and purple, beside a snake's face with pits glowing.

explanations.concept: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays: short waves with big energy
explanations.definition: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have very short wavelengths. Each photon carries a lot of energy, enough to damage living cells.
explanations.description: A photon of ultraviolet light carries more energy than a photon of blue light. It can burn skin, which is why we wear hats and sunscreen at the beach. Bees, and many birds, can see some ultraviolet. X-rays carry even more energy. They pass through soft parts of the body but are stopped by bone, so doctors use them to see inside us. Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling used X-rays in 1952 to take the photograph that helped show the shape of DNA. Marie Curie set up mobile X-ray units in the First World War to help doctors find bullets and broken bones. Because X-rays can harm cells, they are used carefully and only when needed. Gamma rays carry the most energy of all.
examples: A hospital X-ray photo of a broken arm shows white bone against darker soft flesh.
A bee sees patterns on a flower that are invisible to us, because they are painted in ultraviolet.
A dentist moves behind a shield while taking an X-ray picture, since the rays can harm cells in large amounts.
explanations.art: A flower photographed twice, once in ordinary light and once in ultraviolet with a dark bullseye pattern, and an X-ray of a hand.

explanations.concept: Why our eyes see only a thin slice of the family
explanations.description: Our eyes catch light with wavelengths from about 0.0004 to 0.0007 millimetres. That is a very thin slice of the whole family. There are several likely reasons. The Sun gives out most of its light in this slice. The air and water let this slice through, while they block much of the ultraviolet and some of the infrared. A cell that catches visible light needs a certain amount of energy, which is the amount a visible photon carries. Many scientists think animals ended up using this slice because it was bright, and because it could reach the ground. Other animals use different slices. Bees and many birds see some ultraviolet. Pit vipers sense infrared. The reasons are an idea, but they fit what we know.
examples: Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that look plain to us.
Pit vipers sense infrared heat from warm prey in darkness.
Fish in the deep sea see only blue light, because almost nothing else reaches that deep.
explanations.art: A strip of the whole light family with a small window marked humans, a wider window marked bees stretching into ultraviolet and another marked pit vipers reaching into infrared.

explanations.definition: Light carries a tiny push. When light lands on a surface, it pushes that surface a very little. This is called radiation pressure.
explanations.description: Light has energy, and it also carries a small push. James Clerk Maxwell worked out in 1873 that light should push on whatever it lands on. Around 1900, Pyotr Lebedev in Moscow, and Ernest Nichols and Gordon Hull in the United States, measured the push. It is very small. Sunlight pushing on a square metre of a shiny sheet gives a force about the weight of one grain of sugar. Nothing in daily life shows it. But in space, with no air and no friction, a tiny push that never stops can add up. Comets give a clue. The tail of a comet always points away from the Sun, because sunlight and the stream of particles from the Sun push the dust and gas outwards.
examples: A comet's glowing tail always points away from the Sun, even when the comet is heading away from it.
Sunlight pushes slightly on every spacecraft, and engineers must allow for it when they plan its path.
A powerful laser can move a tiny, light mirror in a lab, just by shining on it.
explanations.art: A comet curving round the Sun with its tail always pointing away from the Sun, shown at three places on its path.

explanations.description: A solar sail is a huge, very thin, shiny sheet that catches the push of sunlight. A spacecraft carrying one needs no fuel. In 2010 a Japanese spacecraft called IKAROS unfolded a square sail in space and showed that sailing on sunlight works. In 2019 a small craft called LightSail 2, paid for by The Planetary Society, used sunlight to raise its orbit around the Earth. Some scientists dream of much bigger sails. Breakthrough Starshot, a plan announced in 2016, imagines tiny sail craft pushed by powerful lasers to a nearby star within a human lifetime. Nobody has built it. The engineering is very hard, and many scientists doubt it can be done. It is an idea, but one built on a real push.
examples: IKAROS in 2010 was the first craft to sail on sunlight between planets.
LightSail 2 raised its own orbit around the Earth using only sunlight.
Breakthrough Starshot is a plan to push tiny craft toward another star with lasers.
explanations.art: A thin square silver sail in space with sunlight arrows pushing on it, and a faint dotted line going toward a distant star.

explanations.concept: The oldest light and what it says about the start of everything
explanations.description: Telescopes can detect a faint glow of microwaves coming from every direction in the sky. It is the oldest light there is. It was set free about 380,000 years after the universe began, when the hot young universe cooled enough to let light travel. In the mid-1960s two radio engineers, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, found it by accident. Their antenna in New Jersey kept picking up a steady hiss. They even cleaned out pigeon droppings from the antenna, but the hiss stayed. As the universe grew, the waves of that old light were stretched until they became microwaves. Scientists agree the glow is real and very smooth. They argue about why it is so smooth, and about what came before it.
examples: A tiny part of the hiss and snow between channels on an old analogue TV is said to have come from this old light.
The glow is a little bit warmer in some directions and cooler in others. Those tiny differences are the seeds of galaxies.
The glow is about 3 degrees above absolute zero, the coldest anything can be.
explanations.art: An egg-shaped map of the whole sky in blotches of blue and orange, with the words oldest light in the middle.

perspectives.explanation: The universe began hot and dense and has been growing ever since. A very quick early growth called inflation would explain why the glow is so smooth. Inflation is an idea that fits the measurements well, but it has not been proved.

The smooth glow could be explained in other ways, for example by a universe that bounces and begins again. These ideas are less popular, but they are taken seriously by some, because inflation has not been tested directly.
Nobody knows yet what happened before the glow was set free, or whether the question 'before' even makes sense.

agreed.text: Light spreads out from a small source, so twice as far away it covers four times the area and each patch gets one quarter as much.
agreed.evidence: Photometers, which are instruments for measuring light, have confirmed this again and again with lamps at measured distances, and sunlight arriving at the other planets matches the same rule.

agreed.text: When a surface absorbs light, the light's energy turns into heat, and dark surfaces absorb more sunlight than light-coloured ones.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers on black and white surfaces in the same sunshine show the black one warming faster, and satellites measure the same difference on whole deserts and snowfields.

agreed.text: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are the same kind of wave, with different wavelengths.
agreed.evidence: All of them travel at the same speed in empty space, can be reflected, and can be made and measured with the same equations that Maxwell wrote in the 1860s. Hertz showed in 1887 that radio waves behave just like light.

agreed.text: Our eyes see only a thin slice of the family of light waves, about 0.0004 to 0.0007 millimetres in wavelength.
agreed.evidence: Instruments such as infrared cameras, radio telescopes and X-ray machines detect the other members, and the measurements agree with each other.

agreed.text: Light carries a tiny push, called radiation pressure.
agreed.evidence: Lebedev in 1900 and Nichols and Hull in 1901 measured it, and spacecraft such as IKAROS in 2010 have sailed on it.

agreed.text: The Earth stays at a steady temperature because it gives out as much infrared as it takes in as sunlight, and gases such as carbon dioxide slow that infrared down.
agreed.evidence: Satellites measure the sunlight coming in and the infrared going out. Measurements of the air and sea over many decades agree.

agreed.text: A faint glow of microwaves, the oldest light there is, comes from every direction in the sky.
agreed.evidence: It was found by Penzias and Wilson in the 1960s, and satellites since then have mapped it in great detail.

challenging.claim: Light is only what our eyes can see.
challenging.who: Most people before 1800, who had no way to detect anything else.
challenging.for: For all of history, dark meant no light. Nothing we could feel or see told us otherwise.
challenging.against: In 1800 William Herschel's thermometer warmed up beyond the red end of the colours, where nothing could be seen. Today cameras, radios and X-ray machines detect the rest of the family.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that light is only what we can see, and why Herschel's thermometer changed it.

challenging.claim: Light gets tired and weaker the further it goes.
challenging.for: A far lamp looks dim, and a faraway star looks small and faint.
challenging.against: In clear space, no light is used up. It spreads over a bigger and bigger area, so each patch gets less. Starlight that has travelled for thousands of years still arrives with its energy intact.
challenging.context: This card is about why far-off lights look dim, and whether light fades along the way.

challenging.claim: Heat and light are completely different things that just happen to travel together.
challenging.who: Many scientists in the 1700s, and Herschel himself at first. He called the invisible heating rays calorific rays.
challenging.for: You can feel heat without seeing anything, and you can see light without feeling heat. They seem to be separate.
challenging.against: In the 1830s Macedonio Melloni, an Italian scientist, showed that radiant heat can be reflected and bent just like light. Both are members of one wave family, and light turns into heat when it is absorbed.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the invisible rays beyond red are a different thing from light.

challenging.claim: Light is weightless, so it cannot push anything.
challenging.who: Most people, since we do not notice sunlight pushing us.
challenging.for: Standing in strong sunlight, you feel warmth but no shove. Light has no mass that you can weigh.
challenging.against: Maxwell predicted in 1873 that light pushes, and Lebedev, Nichols and Hull measured the push around 1900. It is tiny, but it moves comet dust and spacecraft sails.
challenging.context: This card is about whether light can push things, even though it has no weight.

challenging.claim: A Crookes radiometer, the little glass bulb with a spinning set of vanes, spins because light pushes on the vanes.
challenging.who: Many people in the 1870s, and many science toy sellers even today.
challenging.for: The vanes spin when light shines on them. It looks like a direct push of light.
challenging.against: The real push of light is far too small to turn the vanes. The radiometer spins best with a little air left inside, and almost stops in a very good vacuum, where light's push would matter most. It spins because the air next to the warm black sides moves.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous toy that seems to show light pushing, and what really turns it.

challenging.claim: Dark surfaces always take in more sunlight than light ones.
challenging.who: Most people, and most textbooks as a rule of thumb.
challenging.for: A black road warms faster than a white wall, and black tanks heat water faster than white ones.
challenging.against: The colour we see tells us only about visible light. Sunlight also has infrared that we cannot see. Some white paints take in a lot of infrared, and some dark 'cool roof' paints reflect it. So the rule is a good one, but not exact.
challenging.context: This card is about the rule that dark things warm up faster in the Sun, and where it stops working.

big_questions.q: Herschel's thermometer warmed up in a place that looked dark. Is a dark place always empty of light?

big_questions.q: When a black road absorbs sunlight, the light seems to disappear. Where did it go?

big_questions.q: The food on your plate holds energy that was sunlight not long ago. Does that make you partly made of sunlight?

big_questions.q: In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a student, spotted the first pulsar in a long paper chart from a radio telescope. Her supervisor shared a Nobel Prize for it in 1974, and she did not. Who should get the credit when a discovery is made by a team?

big_questions.q: Sunlight pushes so little that you do not notice it, yet in space it can move a spacecraft. Does a small push that never stops count for more than a big push that stops?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a very slow push on a swing, repeated at the right moment, can build up.

big_questions.q: Our eyes see only a thin slice of the light family. What else might be happening around us that no animal on Earth can sense?
big_questions.hint: Before the 1800s, nobody knew about radio waves or X-rays. How did people find them?

big_questions.q: The oldest light in the sky left when the universe was very young. If we could see even older light, what would it show?
big_questions.hint: Before the glow was set free, the universe was too hot and dense for light to travel. Can we ever see further back?

how_we_found_out.story: For most of history, people thought sunlight held only the rays their eyes could see, the colours of the rainbow. In 1800, William Herschel, an astronomer living in England, wanted to know if some colours carry more heat than others. He had noticed that coloured glasses on his telescope let through different amounts of warmth. He used a glass prism to spread sunlight into a band of colours on a table. He put a thermometer with a blackened bulb in each colour in turn, and kept two more in the shade nearby as controls. The temperature climbed from violet toward red. Then he moved a thermometer just past the red edge, where nothing could be seen. It got warmest of all. Something invisible was carrying heat. In 1801 Johann Ritter, a German scientist, found invisible rays beyond the violet end too, because they darkened a chemical called silver chloride. Later scientists showed these rays behave like light, and belong to one big family.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the rays in sunlight were only the ones the eye can see, and that the dark place beyond the red end was empty. Herschel's thermometer warmed up there, so something unseen was arriving.

story.title: The Third Thermometer
story.note: A made-up story built on real events. In 1800, William Herschel really did spread sunlight into colours with a prism and measure the heat of each colour with thermometers. He really did find that the thermometer just past the red end got warmest. His sister Caroline, a real astronomer who found comets, lived in his house. Nell Hart, her questions and her part in the discovery are imagined. The words they speak are made up.
text: In the year 1800, in the town of Slough in England, there lived a famous astronomer named William Herschel. Years before, he had found a new planet. Now he lived in a house full of telescopes, brass tubes, mirrors and clocks.

Nell Hart was eleven. She came to the house every morning to help. She polished the brass and carried the tea. Best of all, when Mr Herschel's hands were busy, she wrote his numbers in a big book. Her handwriting was very neat.

One bright morning, Mr Herschel closed the shutters of the sunniest room, and left one thin slit. A bar of sunlight came through. He held a glass prism in it. On the table, the white light spread into a band of colours. Red at one end, then orange, yellow, green, blue and violet at the other. Nell had seen rainbows in the sky. She had never seen one lying on a table.

'Here is my puzzle,' said Mr Herschel. 'When I look at the Sun through my telescope, I put coloured glass in front of my eye. The red glass makes my hand warm. Some other glasses do not. Does each colour of sunlight carry its own amount of heat?'
'How will you find out?' asked Nell.
'With thermometers.'

He set out three. He had painted the glass bulb of each one black with ink, because black takes in light well. The first he would move through the colours, one by one. The second he put far off in the shade, and the third he put in the shade at the side. 'Those two are my controls,' he said. 'They tell us how warm the room is on its own. If the room warms, I must not think the colours did it.'
Nell nodded. It was like keeping one pot of milk off the fire, to see how warm milk gets all by itself.

For an hour they worked. Nell read the numbers and wrote them in the book. The first thermometer, in the violet, climbed a little. In the green it climbed more. In the red it climbed most of all. Everything fitted. Red light was the warmest light, and Mr Herschel nodded as if the puzzle were solved.

But Nell was a girl who liked to check things. She kept glancing at the controls. The one far off in the shade stayed steady, just as it should. But the one standing close to the red edge was not steady. It sat on a patch of table where there was no colour at all, only shadow. And the thin red line in its glass was creeping up.
'Mr Herschel,' she said, 'this thermometer is going wrong. It is in the dark, but it is getting warm.'
'It cannot be going wrong,' he said. 'It is a control. Nothing is shining on it.'
'Then why is it warm?'
Mr Herschel looked at the thermometer. He looked at the far edge of the red. 'The room is not warmer,' he said slowly. 'The other control has not moved.'
'A thermometer cannot warm up by itself,' said Nell. 'The milk only warms if the pot is on the fire. Something must be landing on this one.'

'Something we cannot see,' said Mr Herschel. He took the first thermometer out of the red, and set it down in the dark patch, a hand's width beyond the red edge. They both stared at the red line in the glass. It rose. It rose past the number for the red. It kept rising until it stood higher than it had stood in any colour at all.
'It is warmer than the red,' whispered Nell. 'And there is no light there.'
Mr Herschel put down his pen. 'There are rays coming from the Sun,' he said, 'that my eyes cannot see.'
Nell wrote the number in the book. Underneath it, in her best handwriting, she wrote: 'The dark place was not empty.'

That evening, walking home, she held out her palm in the last of the sunshine. The warmth lay on her hand like a coin. She wondered how many more rays were falling on it that she would never see. The sky, she thought, was full of messengers, and her eyes were listening to only a few of them.

Mr Herschel wrote up what he had found, and it was printed for other scientists to read. In the years after, others went looking in the dark places beyond the colours. Beyond the violet they found more invisible rays. Later people found radio waves, and then X-rays. Each time, someone had put a detector where the eye saw nothing.
story.epiphany: A thermometer in a place that looked dark got warm. So something unseen was arriving. Our eyes catch only a slice of the light that reaches us.

roots.context: We found that light spreads out, turns into heat, and belongs to a long family of waves. Now we ask what that tells us about what we can see, and what is there when we cannot see it.

deep_truth.truth: The thermometer beyond the red end of the colours warmed up, though that place looked dark. Our eyes catch only a thin slice of one long family of waves. The rest still reaches us and still does things. So 'dark' tells us what our eyes miss, not what is there.
deep_truth.habit: We treat the edge of what we can sense as the edge of what exists, and call whatever lies past it nothing.
deep_truth.evidence: In the remote control test, your eyes saw nothing coming from the remote, but a phone camera showed it flickering. In 1800 Herschel's thermometer warmed in a place that looked dark. If your phone shows nothing, write that down honestly and try another camera.

three.who_am_i: You are warm right now, so you are giving out infrared. A thermal camera would show you glowing, even in a dark room.
three.what_is_life: A pit viper senses a warm mouse by the infrared the mouse gives out, in total darkness. A bee steers by ultraviolet patterns on flowers. Each living being senses their own slice of the family of light.
three.what_is_this_world: The room you sit in is full of radio waves, microwaves and infrared passing through it. Whether a place seems empty depends on what you are able to sense.

roots.thread: Radio waves, infrared, visible light and X-rays are one kind of wave in different sizes. What we call light is the slice our eyes happen to catch. Our skin catches the next slice as warmth, though we call that feeling and not seeing. Each animal has their own slice. So what any one of us sees is a small part of what reaches us, and the world holds more than any one creature can sense.

teachings.teaching: Plato, an ancient Greek thinker, told of prisoners chained in a cave since birth, who see only shadows on the wall in front of them. They think the shadows are the whole world. A prisoner who climbs out is dazzled by the real things.
teachings.link: The prisoners treat the edge of what they can see as the edge of the world. The thermometer beyond the red end of the colours showed the same mistake about light.

teachings.teaching: The Katha Upanishad says that the Sun does not shine there, nor the moon, nor the stars, nor lightning, much less this fire. It says that all things shine after something that shines, and that by that light all this is lit.
teachings.link: This unit followed sunlight to its end, to heat and to the waves our eyes cannot see. The Upanishad points to something behind all lights. Science cannot test that. It can only show that the light we see is one slice among many.

science.text: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are one family of waves that differ in wavelength.
Our eyes are tuned to the thin slice of the family that the Sun gives out most and the air lets through. This is a good explanation but not proven for every animal.
What happened before the oldest light in the sky was set free is not known.

other_view.view: The family of waves is a physical fact and nothing more. Words like 'dark' and 'visible' describe our eyes, not the world. There is no deeper lesson about the limits of knowing hiding in it. This is an honest view.

practice.title: Feel the light you cannot see
practice.say: Sit near a sunny window, or beside a warm steel tumbler. Close your eyes. Hold your palm toward the warmth, without touching anything. Breathe in for a count of four. Breathe out for a count of four. Feel the warmth on your palm. Your eyes cannot see this light, but your skin can feel it. Breathe in once more. Open your eyes and look slowly around the room.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Hold your palm toward the warmth. Breathe in four counts and out four counts. Feel the light you cannot see.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: something from daily life on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: Your FM radio plays a song from the All India Radio station in Chennai.
items.b: Radio waves. FM radio waves are about 3 metres long, the longest waves in the family.

items.f: A TV station sends a cricket match to the aerial on your roof.
items.b: Radio waves. TV signals travel as radio waves, which pass through walls and clouds.

items.f: Mission control at ISRO talks to a spacecraft far out in space.
items.b: Radio waves. They cross empty space at the speed of light, and a big dish can catch them. Some space signals use the short end of the radio range, which many people call microwaves.

items.f: A giant dish near Pune listens to a spinning dead star far away.
items.b: Radio waves. Radio telescopes catch the long waves that stars and galaxies send out.

items.f: Wi-Fi carries a video to a tablet in the next room.
items.b: Microwaves. Wi-Fi waves are about 12 centimetres long.

items.f: A mobile phone sends your voice to a tower down the road.
items.b: Microwaves. The line between radio and microwaves is a matter of choice, and phone signals sit near it.

items.f: A microwave oven warms last night's sambar.
items.b: Microwaves. In an oven they shake the water in the food, and the shaking makes heat.

items.f: The oldest light in the universe is still arriving from every direction in the sky.
items.b: Microwaves. It left as visible and infrared light, and the stretching of space made its waves much longer.

items.f: You feel the warmth of a lit stove on your face from a metre away.
items.b: Infrared. Warm things give out infrared, and your skin feels it as warmth.

items.f: A TV remote changes the channel when you press a button.
items.b: Infrared. The remote sends a quick pattern of invisible flickers that the TV reads.

items.f: A thermal camera shows a warm person walking in a dark street.
items.b: Infrared. The camera turns the infrared from warm bodies into a coloured picture.

items.f: A pit viper finds a warm mouse in total darkness.
items.b: Infrared. The snake has small pits on her face that sense infrared.

items.f: A rainbow shines in the sky after the monsoon rain.
items.b: Visible light. This is the slice of the family that our eyes can see, from red to violet.

items.f: A diya flame lights up a dark room.
items.b: Visible light. The hot flame gives out visible light as well as infrared.

items.f: A firefly flashes in the garden at night.
items.b: Visible light. The firefly makes the light with a chemical reaction in her body.

items.f: A green leaf catches sunlight to make food.
items.b: Visible light. Leaves use mostly the red and blue parts of visible light.

items.f: You get sunburnt after a long day at the beach.
items.b: Ultraviolet. Ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to damage skin cells.

items.f: A bee spots a pattern on a flower that people cannot see.
items.b: Ultraviolet. Many flowers have patterns that show up only in ultraviolet light, which bees can see.

items.f: A black light makes a white shirt glow at a party.
items.b: Ultraviolet. A black light gives out mostly ultraviolet, which our eyes cannot see, and some cloth glows when it takes it in.

items.f: A doctor studies a photograph of a broken arm bone.
items.b: X-rays. They pass through soft flesh but are stopped by bone, so bone shows up white.

items.f: A machine at the airport looks inside your bags.
items.b: X-rays. Bags are scanned with X-rays that pass through cloth but are stopped by metal.

items.f: Doctors aim a narrow beam from a radioactive source at a tumour.
items.b: Gamma rays. The strong, short waves can kill harmful cells, so doctors aim them carefully.

items.f: A star explodes far away and a space telescope catches a flash of the strongest waves there are.
items.b: Gamma rays. They are the shortest waves in the family and carry the most energy.

items.f: Mangoes sent abroad are sometimes treated with a beam to kill pests.
items.b: Gamma rays, in many cases. The beam does not make the food radioactive, and the food is kept in a sealed room while it is treated.

printables.title: The Family Line: 7 signs to cut out and lay in a row
Paper stars, buttons or coins to count points (48 are enough)
items: Cut out 48 small paper stars, or use buttons or coins

rules: Lay the 7 signs of the Family Line in a row, with radio waves at the left and gamma rays at the right. This is the order from the longest waves to the shortest.
Shuffle the 24 cards and make a face-down pile. Put the 48 stars in a heap in the middle.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front aloud. Do not read the back.
Say which sign you think the card belongs under, and why. Put the card under that sign.
Now read the back aloud. If you picked the right sign, take 2 stars. If you were wrong, move the card to the right sign and take 1 star for any good reason.
Play until all 24 cards are placed. The player with the most stars wins. If you tie, you share the win.
Playing alone: try to put at least 18 of the 24 cards under the right sign on the first go, then play again to beat your score.

flow.parent: Good reasons are about what the thing does. Messages, warmth, sight and doctor's tools sit in different places. Credit a good reason even when the sign is wrong.

check.q: Which waves in the family carry the most energy in each photon?
options: The shortest waves, gamma rays
The longest waves, radio waves
All of them carry the same
The visible ones in the middle
check.why: The shorter the wavelength, the more energy each photon carries. Gamma rays are the shortest, so they carry the most. items.b: 5 lanterns. One lantern gives 4 at 6 steps (144 ÷ 36). 5 lanterns give 20, which is enough. With 4, you would get only 16, which is too little.

items.b: 1 lantern. One lantern gives 1 at 12 steps (144 ÷ 144). 1 lantern gives 1, which is enough.

items.b: 3 lanterns. One lantern gives 1 at 12 steps (144 ÷ 144). 3 lanterns give 3, which is enough. With 2, you would get only 2, which is too little.

items.b: 5 lanterns. One lantern gives 1 at 12 steps (144 ÷ 144). 5 lanterns give 5, which is enough. With 4, you would get only 4, which is too little.
