printables.title: The Lantern Light Table: 6 rows
items: 1 step from the lantern post: one lantern gives 144

printables.title: Paper stars, buttons or coins to count points (48 are enough)
items: Cut out 48 small paper stars, or use buttons or coins

rules: Put the Lantern Light Table where everyone can see it. It shows how much light one lantern gives at each distance. Light is counted in light units.
Shuffle the 24 stall cards and make a face-down pile. Put the 48 stars in a heap in the middle.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front aloud. Do not read the back.
Work out how many lanterns the post needs, so that the stall gets at least the light it needs. Say your number and show your working.
Read the back. If your number is exactly right, take 2 stars. If you hung one lantern too many, take 1 star. If you hung too few, take none.
Play until the cards run out. The player with the most stars wins. If you tie, you share the win.
Playing alone: score 2 stars for each exact answer. Try for 36 stars out of 48.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the table. Read the table together and point to what happens to one lantern's light as the stall moves further away.
flow.say: One lantern gives 144 light units one step away. Look at what it gives two steps away. And four steps away. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Read the table. What happens to the light as the stall moves away?
flow.context: This is the first step of Lantern Stalls. You look at the table of how light thins out.

ask.q: What happens to the light when the distance doubles from 1 step to 2 steps?

flow.parent: 144 divided by 4 is 36. And 36 divided by 4 is 9, when the distance doubles again from 2 to 4. The light falls to one quarter each time the distance doubles.

flow.do: Try two cards together. Work out the number of lanterns and check the back.
flow.say: Let's try a card together. How much light does one lantern give at this stall? How many do we need?
flow.kid: Try a card together. How much light does one lantern give there?
flow.context: In this step, you try two practice cards and learn how the stars work.

check.q: A stall is 4 steps from the post. One lantern gives 9 there. The stall needs a light of at least 20. How many lanterns?
options: 3 lanterns
2 lanterns
1 lantern
4 lanterns
check.why: One lantern gives 9, two give 18 and three give 27. Two give 18, which is less than 20. Three give 27, which is enough. Picking 2 is the common slip, because 18 looks close to 20, but close is not enough.

flow.do: Take turns. Each player takes a card, works out the lanterns, shows the working, then reads the back. Give stars as the rules say.
flow.say: Read your card. How much does one lantern give at this stall? How many do you need? Tell us your working.
flow.kid: Take turns. Work out the lanterns, show your working, then check the back.
flow.context: In this step, you play the main part of Lantern Stalls, card by card.
flow.parent: If your child gets stuck, ask: how much does one lantern give? Then count up in that number until you reach the light needed.
flow.think: The stall at 12 steps needs 12 lanterns for a light of 12. Why do far stalls need so many?

flow.do: Count the stars. Then ask the question about the pattern.
flow.say: A stall twice as far away needs how many times as many lanterns, to get the same light? Check with the cards.
flow.kid: A stall twice as far needs how many times as many lanterns?
flow.context: In this step, you find the rule behind the table.

check.q: A stall moves from 2 steps to 4 steps from the post. About how many times as many lanterns does it need for the same light?
options: 4 times as many
2 times as many
The same number
8 times as many
check.why: At double the distance, each lantern gives one quarter as much light. So you need four times as many lanterns to get the same light. Picking 2 is a common slip, because the distance doubled, but light spreads over an area, and the area is four times bigger.

flow.do: Talk about how people solve this in real life. Lighthouses, torches and car headlights gather light into a beam.
flow.say: Four times as many lanterns are needed at double the distance. How could you send more light to a far stall, without more lanterns?
flow.kid: How could you send more light to a far stall?
flow.context: In this step, you think of ways to keep light from spreading.
flow.think: A mirror behind a lantern sends light forward. A lens can gather it too. Would either help a far stall?

experiments.title: Torch Spread: how fast does a beam thin out?
experiments.question: A torch lights a square patch on squared paper. If the paper is moved twice as far from the torch, how many times bigger is the lit patch, and how bright does it look?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you move the paper twice as far from the torch, how many times bigger will the lit patch be? Will it look brighter, dimmer or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The torch, the card with the square hole and the dark room stay the same every time. The torch stays 10 centimetres behind the card. Only the distance from the torch to the paper changes: 20, 30 and 40 centimetres. Measure every distance from the bulb itself (on a phone, the small lamp next to the camera), not from the end of the torch. Do each distance twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: How many times bigger than the patch at 20 cm (divide the area by the area at 20 cm)
How bright the patch looked: brightest, dimmer or dimmest

materials.item: a phone torch (best, because its light comes from a tiny LED) or a small LED torch with a bare bulb. A torch with a big mirror or lens makes a narrow beam and will not give this result
a piece of thin card about 15 centimetres square, from a cereal box, with a square hole exactly 2 centimetres by 2 centimetres cut in the middle
squared paper with 1 centimetre squares, such as a maths notebook page, taped flat to a book or a wall
a ruler or tape measure that reads in centimetres
a pencil and some modelling clay or sticky tape to hold the card upright
a room that can be made very dark, such as one with curtains closed in the evening

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the square hole with scissors. Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the torch, the card with the hole and the paper at 20, 30 and 40 centimetres, with the lit patch drawn on each paper. Write the area under each one.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you shine a torch through a square hole in a card onto squared paper. You measure how the lit patch grows when the paper moves away, and see what happens to its brightness.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: area of the lit patch
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be a little different.

setup.art: A torch standing on a table pointing at a card with a small square hole, 10 centimetres behind the card, with a ruler lying along the table.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the card with the square hole 10 centimetres in front of the torch.

setup.art: Squared paper taped to a book 20 centimetres from the torch, with a small lit square of 4 by 4 squares on it.
setup.caption: 2. Put squared paper 20 centimetres from the torch. Count the squares that are lit.

setup.art: The same set-up with the paper moved to 40 centimetres, where the lit patch is larger and fainter, covering 8 by 8 squares.
setup.caption: 3. Move the paper to 30 and then 40 centimetres. Count the lit squares again.

setup.art: Three pieces of squared paper side by side with lit patches of increasing size, labelled 20, 30 and 40 centimetres.
setup.caption: 4. Compare the three patches. How many times bigger is each? How bright does each look?

flow.do: Show your child the torch, the card with the hole and the squared paper. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will shine a torch through a small square hole in a card. The light makes a square patch on squared paper. If we move the paper twice as far away, how big will the patch be? Will it look brighter or dimmer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A torch shines through a small square hole. Move the paper twice as far away. How big is the patch? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the patch will change that way?
good: It will be twice as big because the distance is twice as big.
The light gets weaker when it goes further.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess twice as big, because the distance is twice as big. That is a very good guess to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Torch Spread test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a 2 centimetre square hole in the middle of the card. Stand the card upright with clay. Place the torch 10 centimetres behind the card, pointing at the hole. Tape squared paper flat to a book.
flow.say: The hole is 2 centimetres wide and 2 centimetres tall. The torch is 10 centimetres behind it. Only the light that goes through the hole will reach the paper.
flow.kid: Cut a 2 centimetre square hole in the card. Stand it up. Put the torch 10 centimetres behind it.
flow.parent: Use a ruler to check the 10 centimetres, because the whole test depends on it. A phone torch works best if you tape it flat so that it does not roll. Block any spill of light around the edges of the card with your hand or a book.

check.q: Why must the torch stay exactly 10 centimetres behind the card every time?
options: So that only the distance to the paper changes
So that the torch looks tidy
So that the torch battery lasts longer
So that the card does not fall over
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the torch moved, the patch would change for two reasons, and you could not tell which. Picking 'the torch looks tidy' mixes up neat with fair.

flow.context: In this step, you make the card and fix the torch. Everything you fix here stays the same during the test.

flow.do: Make the room very dark. Put the squared paper 20 centimetres from the torch. Switch on the torch. Count the squares across and down in the lit patch. Write them in the table. Repeat once more.
flow.say: Look at the lit patch. How many squares wide is it? How many tall? Count the squares that are mostly lit. How bright does it look?
flow.kid: Switch the torch on in the dark. Count the lit squares across and down. Write the numbers down.
flow.parent: At 20 centimetres, the patch should be about 4 squares wide and 4 tall, so about 16 squares. The edges are a little blurry because the torch bulb is not a tiny dot. Count a square if it is more than half lit.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the lit patch at 20 centimetres from the torch. This is your starting number.

flow.do: Move the paper to 30 centimetres. Count the lit squares. Write them down. Repeat once. Then move the paper to 40 centimetres, count, and repeat once. Compare the brightness each time.
flow.say: Move the paper further away. Count the squares again. Is the patch bigger? How much bigger? Is it as bright as before?
flow.kid: Move the paper to 30 centimetres. Count the squares. Then move it to 40 centimetres. Count again.
flow.parent: Expected: about 6 by 6 squares at 30 centimetres, which is 36, and about 8 by 8 squares at 40 centimetres, which is 64. Real counts are often a bit bigger because of the blur. If your numbers are different, write them down as they are. The patch at 40 centimetres should look dimmer than the one at 20. If the patch is much bigger or oddly shaped, the usual reasons are a room that is not dark enough, a torch that is not exactly 10 centimetres behind the card, or a torch with a lens. Fix that and repeat. Judging brightness by eye is rough, so ask a second person to say which patch looks dimmer without knowing the distances. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the paper steady, one keeps the torch still, one counts squares and one writes, and they swap for each distance. One child alone: tape the paper to a book propped on a stack and tape the torch down, so both stay still.

check.q: The patch at 20 centimetres covers about 16 squares. The paper moves to 40 centimetres, twice as far. About how many squares are lit?
options: About 64 squares, four times as many
About 32 squares, twice as many
About 16 squares, the same
About 8 squares, half as many
check.why: Twice as far makes the patch twice as wide and twice as tall. Two times two is four, so it covers four times the area: 16 times 4 is 64. Picking 32 is the common guess, because the distance doubled. That forgets the patch grows in two directions at once.

flow.context: In this step, you move the paper further away and count the lit squares again.

flow.do: Look at the three patches. Ask how many times bigger the patch at 40 centimetres is than at 20. Ask how much of the torch's light each square gets at 40 centimetres. Draw the results.
flow.say: The same torch light went through the same hole. At 40 centimetres, it covered four times as many squares. So each square got how much of the light, compared with 20 centimetres?
flow.kid: The same light covered more squares. Did each square get more light or less?

ask.q: Is the light on the far paper used up, or just spread out?
good: It is spread out over more squares.
The same light is shared by more squares.
Each square gets a quarter as much.

ask.q: Where would the patch be nine times bigger?

flow.parent: The key idea is that the amount of light going through the hole did not change. It was spread over four times the area, so each square got one quarter as much. This is why a far lamp looks dim even though it has not changed.

check.q: At 40 centimetres the patch covers four times the area it covered at 20. What can you say about each square of the far patch?
options: It gets about one quarter as much light
It gets four times as much light
It gets the same light as before
It gets no light
check.why: The same light is shared by four times as many squares. So each square gets one quarter as much. Picking 'four times as much' mixes up bigger patch with more light. A bigger patch has the same light spread more thinly.

flow.context: In this step, you work out what the bigger patch means for the brightness of each part of it.

experiments.title: Ice Race: where does the light go?
experiments.question: Four ice cubes sit in the same sunshine on black paper, dark blue paper, yellow paper and white paper. Which melts first, and which melts last?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which ice cube will melt first and which last? Will the cube in the shade melt at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the cubes come from the same ice tray, so they are the same size. All the papers are the same size, and all sit side by side on one piece of thick cardboard in the same sunshine. Only the colour of the paper changes. Paper is thin, so the cardboard underneath keeps a hot steel tray or a white wall from changing the result. A fifth cube sits on white paper in the shade as the control, so you know what the room alone does.
results_table: In the sun or in the shade
Size of the cube after 5 minutes: whole, big, half, small or gone
Minutes until the cube was gone

materials.item: 5 ice cubes of the same size from one ice tray, kept in the freezer until the last moment, carried in a steel box or a flask. Pick the five that look most alike
5 squares of paper, each 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres: 1 black, 1 dark blue, 1 yellow and 2 white
a piece of thick cardboard, such as a cut-open carton or a wooden board, to carry the papers (not a steel tray, which heats up and muddles the test)
a sunny windowsill, balcony or terrace where direct sun falls on the tray for 20 minutes
a phone timer or a clock
a pencil

experiments.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Do the test on a sunny day. An LED lamp gives out too little heat, and a hot bulb is not safe for children to use. Surfaces left in the sun can get hot, so touch them with care. Keep to shade and a hat if the sun is very strong.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each paper, showing how many minutes the cube lasted. Write which colour melted its cube first and which last.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you place ice cubes on black, blue, yellow and white paper in the sunshine. You find out which colour makes the ice melt first, and what that shows about what colours do with light.

setup.art: A piece of thick cardboard in a patch of sunshine on a windowsill, with four squares of paper in black, dark blue, yellow and white, and one more white square on cardboard in the shade beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the papers on the cardboard in the sun. Put the fifth white paper in the shade.

setup.art: A child placing an ice cube on each square of paper, one after another, using a steel spoon, with a phone timer showing zero.
setup.caption: 2. Put one ice cube on each paper at the same moment. Start the timer.

setup.art: The tray after 10 minutes, with the cube on black paper almost gone, the cubes on blue and yellow half melted and the one on white still big.
setup.caption: 3. Look every 5 minutes. Write down how big each cube is.

setup.art: A bar chart drawn on paper beside the tray, with a tall bar for white paper and a short bar for black paper.
setup.caption: 4. Draw a bar for each paper to show how long its cube lasted.

flow.do: Show your child the five papers, the cardboard and the ice. Ask for a guess and a reason about which cube melts first and last. Write it at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will put ice cubes on black, blue, yellow and white paper in the sunshine. Which one will melt first? Which one will melt last? What about the cube in the shade? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Ice cubes on four colours in the sun. Which melts first? Which last? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that colour will melt its cube first?
good: Black gets hotter in the sun.
Dark colours soak up more sun.
Light colours bounce the sun away.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The cube in the shade is the control. It shows how fast ice melts with no sunshine at all.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ice Race. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Choose a spot in direct sun. Lay the black, blue, yellow and white papers on the cardboard, with a gap between them. Put the cardboard flat in the sun, out of the wind. Lay the fifth white paper, on another piece of cardboard, in the shade next to it.
flow.say: Sun on four papers, and shade on one. The cardboard must sit in the same sunshine, so no paper gets more sun than another.
flow.kid: Put four papers on the cardboard in the sun. Put one white paper in the shade.
flow.parent: Check that no shadow of a window frame falls across the cardboard. Direct sun at midday or in the early afternoon works best. If the sun is weak or the day is cloudy, wait for a sunnier day. The test needs direct sunshine. White paper is a little see-through, so put it on white card or a plain page if the cardboard shows through. With 2 to 4 children: each child looks after one colour and its timer or tally, and one watches the control.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the tray in the sun with the control in the shade.

flow.do: Bring the ice cubes out only now. Use a spoon to put one on each paper, in the middle. Start the timer as you put down the last one. Look at the cubes at 5 minutes. Write down their sizes.
flow.say: Ice on all five papers. The timer is running. Watch closely. At 5 minutes, which cube looks smallest? Which looks the biggest?
flow.kid: Put one ice cube on each paper. Start the timer. Look again at 5 minutes.
flow.parent: Use the same words every time for the sizes: whole, big, half, small, gone. If the cubes slide, set them back in the middle. Do not shake the cardboard.
flow.context: In this step, you start the ice race and look at the cubes after 5 minutes.

flow.do: Look again at 10 minutes and at 15 minutes. Write down the sizes. Keep looking every few minutes until each cube is gone. Write the minute each cube disappeared.
flow.say: Which cube is gone first? Which is last? Write down the minute for each one. Is the cube in the shade melting at all?
flow.kid: Look at 10 and 15 minutes. Write how big each cube is. Note when each one is gone.
flow.parent: Expected: the cube on black melts first, the cubes on dark blue and yellow come in between, and white lasts longest. The shaded cube melts slowest of all. Typical times in strong Indian sun are about 10 to 25 minutes, and the gap between black and white is often only a few minutes, so look closely. Your times will differ. If all the cubes melt at nearly the same time, the sun was weak or the cubes were not alike. Try again on a sunnier day with fresh cubes. Melted water can make the paper soggy. That is fine, but keep each cube in the middle of its paper.

check.q: Why do we keep a cube on white paper in the shade?
options: To see how fast ice melts without any sunshine
To make the race look fair
To cool the other cubes down
To use up the spare paper
check.why: The shaded cube is the control. It shows what the room does to ice by itself. If the cubes in the sun melt faster than the control, the sunshine did the extra melting. Picking 'to cool the other cubes' is wrong, because the shaded cube is too far away to cool anything.

flow.context: In this step, you watch the cubes melt and write down the time for each.

flow.do: Compare the times. Draw the bar chart. Ask what the different colours do with the sunlight that falls on them.
flow.say: Black melted its ice first. White lasted longest. The same sunlight landed on every paper. So what must the colours have done with it?
flow.kid: The same sunlight landed on every paper. What did black do with it? What did white do?

ask.q: Where did the light that landed on the black paper go?
good: The paper took in the light and got warm.

flow.parent: The paper that absorbs more light turns more of it to heat, and the heat melts the ice. The white paper reflects much of the light, so less becomes heat. Energy is not lost. It changes from light to heat.

check.q: The ice melted fastest on black paper. What does this tell you about black paper and sunlight?
options: It takes in more of the light and turns it into heat
It makes its own heat
It sends more light back
It makes the Sun hotter
check.why: Black paper absorbs most of the sunlight that lands on it, and the light's energy becomes heat. Picking 'it sends more light back' is the opposite. White paper does that. Picking 'it makes its own heat' mixes up making heat with turning light into heat.

flow.context: In this step, you explain the race: what black and white paper do with sunlight.

experiments.title: The Invisible Flicker: what does a TV remote send out?
experiments.question: A TV remote sends a signal to the TV, and your eyes see nothing. Can a phone camera see what the remote sends, and does that signal go through things and bounce off things like light?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When you look at the remote through a phone camera, will you see anything? Will the signal go through a piece of paper? Will it bounce off a mirror? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same remote, the same button and the same distance from the camera, 20 centimetres, every time. Keep the room dim so any flicker is easy to see. Only the thing you put in the way changes. A test with nothing in the way is the control.
results_table: Did the flicker show on the phone screen: yes, faint or no?
Mirror and wall test only: did the TV obey the remote: yes or no?

materials.item: a TV remote that works with infrared, such as most TV, air conditioner or set-top box remotes, with working batteries. Remotes that need no aiming, or that have a voice button (many smart TV and streaming-stick remotes), use Bluetooth radio and will show nothing, so choose an ordinary one with a small dark window at the front
a phone with a camera, preferably the front camera that you use for selfies
a sheet of thin paper, a piece of thick card, a steel plate or lid, and a glass tumbler, to put in the way
a small mirror, such as a pocket mirror or a hand mirror
a TV or other device that obeys the remote
a dim room, such as one with curtains drawn

experiments.safety: Do not open the remote. Keep batteries away from young children, who must not put them in their mouths. The invisible light from a remote is harmless to your eyes.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the remote, the phone and a wavy line between them, and write what you saw on the screen.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you look at a TV remote through a phone camera. You find out whether the remote sends out invisible light, and whether it behaves like the light you can see.

setup.art: A TV remote held 20 centimetres from a phone camera in a dim room, with a button being pressed.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the remote 20 centimetres from the phone camera. Look at the screen, not the remote.

setup.art: The phone screen showing a pale purple-white flicker at the front of the remote when the button is pressed.
setup.caption: 2. Press a button. Look for a flicker at the front of the remote.

setup.art: A sheet of paper, a piece of card and a steel plate held one at a time in front of the remote while the phone screen shows the flicker.
setup.caption: 3. Put paper, card and steel in the way, one at a time. Does the flicker still show?

setup.art: A child aiming a remote at a small mirror held beside the TV so the signal bounces off the mirror onto the TV.
setup.caption: 4. Aim the remote at a mirror, so the signal bounces to the TV.

flow.do: Show your child the remote, the phone and the mirror. Ask for guesses and reasons about what the camera will show. Write them in the table notes.
flow.say: A remote controls the TV from across the room, and you cannot see anything leaving it. Will the phone camera see anything? Will paper block it? Will a mirror bounce it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A remote sends a signal you cannot see. Will a phone camera see it? Why?

ask.q: What do you think leaves the front of the remote?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Remote controls use infrared, which is light just beyond red. Your child's eyes cannot see it. The test shows whether a camera can.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Invisible Flicker test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Dim the room. First look at the front of the remote with your own eyes, and press a button. Then switch on the phone's front camera. Hold the remote 20 centimetres from it. Press a button while looking at the screen.
flow.say: First, look at the front of the remote with just your eyes. Press a button. What do you see? Now look through the phone's camera. What do you see now?
flow.kid: Look at the remote with your eyes. Press a button. Now look through the phone.
flow.parent: Expected: nothing with the eyes, and a pale purple or white flicker on the screen. The front camera of most phones shows it. Some rear cameras have a filter that hides it. If you see nothing, try another phone, the front camera or a laptop webcam, or another remote (a different brand often shows it). If nothing works, write that down honestly. The TV test in step 4 still works, because the TV is the detector. One child alone: lean the phone against a book so it stands by itself, and hold the remote in one hand. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the phone, one presses the button, one holds the things in the way, and one writes. Swap roles.

check.q: Your eyes saw nothing from the remote, but the phone camera showed a flicker. What is the best explanation?
options: The remote sends light that our eyes cannot see, but the camera can
The camera is making the flicker up
The remote is not sending anything
The remote is sending sound
check.why: A camera chip catches some light that our eyes miss. The remote sends infrared, just beyond red. Picking 'the camera is making it up' is a common idea, but the flicker appears only when the button is pressed, and it follows the remote around, so it comes from the remote.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the remote with your eyes, and then through a phone camera.

flow.do: Keep the remote 20 centimetres from the camera. Put the paper in front of the remote, then the card, then the steel plate, then the glass tumbler. Press a button each time and write down what the screen shows.
flow.say: Put the paper in the way. Does the flicker still show? Now try the thick card, then steel, then glass. Which ones let the invisible light through?
flow.kid: Put things in front of the remote one by one. Does the flicker still show?
flow.parent: Results vary with the remote and the room, so write what you see. Often thin paper lets some through and looks fainter, thick card and steel block most of it, and clear glass lets it through. Do not worry if yours differ. Press the button three times for each thing, because one press can be missed.
flow.context: In this step, you find out which things the invisible light goes through and which things block it.

flow.do: Face the TV and hold the mirror to one side. Aim the remote at the mirror. Tilt the mirror so that it points to the TV. Press the button and see if the TV obeys. Then try aiming at a white wall beside the TV.
flow.say: Can we bounce the remote's signal to the TV with a mirror? Aim at the mirror and tilt it toward the TV. Does the TV obey? Does a wall work too?
flow.kid: Aim the remote at the mirror. Tilt it toward the TV. Does the TV obey?
flow.parent: A tilted mirror often works, because the invisible light reflects off the mirror just like visible light. A pale wall near the TV may also work, because the wall scatters some of the light onto the TV. If the TV does not obey, try getting closer and aiming more carefully.
flow.context: In this step, you try to bounce the remote's invisible light off a mirror and a wall, to see if it behaves like ordinary light.

flow.do: Compare the results with what you guessed. Ask what the experiment shows about the light we can see.
flow.say: The remote sends light that we cannot see. It goes through some things, gets blocked by others, and bounces off a mirror. So what is it like?
flow.kid: The remote sends light you cannot see. Does it act like light you can see?

ask.q: What did the camera show that your eyes could not?
good: That there is light beyond what we can see.

flow.parent: This is the same lesson as Herschel's thermometer. There is light that our eyes do not catch, and other instruments can show it.

check.q: The remote's signal bounced off a mirror and was blocked by a steel plate. What does this suggest about it?
options: It behaves like light, though we cannot see it
It behaves like sound
It is not real
It is made by the mirror
check.why: Reflecting off mirrors and being blocked by solid things are things light does. Sound would bend round a plate and fill a room. Picking 'it is not real' is a slip, because the TV obeyed it, so it was doing something.

flow.context: In this step, you decide what the remote's signal is like, using what you found.

activities.title: Light's Jobs: what does sunlight do around our home?

materials.item: a sunny window, balcony or doorway
a piece of black cloth and a piece of white cloth of the same kind (both cotton, for example), each about the size of a handkerchief
paper and a pencil
a solar calculator, solar garden lamp or similar, if you have one

schedule.what: Hunt for the jobs light does at home, feel the warmth of light, and sort the jobs.

activities.record: A list of at least eight jobs that light does at home, with a note on what the light turns into for each one: heat, sugar, electricity or something else.
activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Keep time in strong midday sun short, and wear a hat.
activities.context: In this activity, you hunt around your home for jobs that light does. You find out that light does much more than help us see.

setup.art: A child with a notebook at a sunny window, pointing at clothes drying on a line outside.
setup.caption: 1. Walk around the home and write down every job that light is doing.

setup.art: A child's hand in a patch of sunshine on the windowsill beside a hand in the shade, with a question mark between them.
setup.caption: 2. Feel the warmth of a patch of sunshine and a patch of shade.

setup.art: A black cloth and a white cloth lying side by side in the sun, with a hand touching each.
setup.caption: 3. Leave a black cloth and a white cloth in the sun, then touch both.

flow.do: Walk around the home with your child. Look for jobs that sunlight or lamp light is doing. Write each one down. Look at the clothes line, the plants, the curtains, the wall calendar and any solar gadget.
flow.say: Light lets us see. What else is light doing in our home right now? Look at the clothes on the line, the plants and the curtains. What is the Sun doing to each?
flow.kid: Walk around the home. What jobs is light doing? Write down eight.

ask.q: Which job of light is hardest to notice?

flow.parent: Possible jobs: drying clothes, warming a patch of floor, feeding the plants, fading a curtain or a calendar, running a solar lamp or calculator, heating water in a rooftop tank, making shadows, and letting us see. If you have a solar calculator, cover its panel with a finger and watch the numbers fade.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Light's Jobs hunt. You look for what light is doing around you.

flow.do: Hold your palm in a patch of sunshine for 20 seconds. Then hold it in the shade for 20 seconds. Say what is different. Then close your eyes and feel which side of your face is toward the window.
flow.say: Put your hand in the sunshine for 20 seconds. What do you feel? Now put it in the shade. What is different? The light is landing on your skin. What is it turning into?
flow.kid: Put your hand in the sun for 20 seconds. Then in the shade. What do you feel?
flow.parent: Choose a gentle sun, not noon sun in summer. Keep it short. The warmth you feel is light that your skin absorbed, turned into heat. Do not look straight at the Sun.
flow.context: In this step, you feel sunlight turn into heat on your own skin.

flow.do: Lay the black cloth and the white cloth side by side on the same flat surface in direct sun for 10 minutes. Guess which will feel warmer first. Then touch each with the back of your hand, eyes closed if a helper moves your hand, and say which feels warmer. Write what you find next to the jobs list.
flow.say: Black cloth and white cloth have been in the sun for the same time. Touch each. Which feels warmer? What is the black cloth doing with the light that the white cloth is not?
flow.kid: Leave two cloths in the sun for 10 minutes. Touch them both. Which is warmer?
flow.parent: In direct sun the black cloth usually feels clearly warmer. On a cloudy or damp day the difference is small, so repeat on a sunny day. Black absorbs more light. White reflects more. Keep this finding. The Ice Race experiment tests it much more carefully. With 2 to 4 children: each one searches a different room or the balcony in step 1, then they share lists, and each child touches the cloths blind in turn.

check.q: The black cloth felt warmer than the white one after the same time in the sun. Why?
options: Black takes in more of the light and turns it into heat
Black makes more light than white does
The Sun shines harder on black things
White cloth is thicker
check.why: Black cloth absorbs most of the light that lands on it, and the energy of the light becomes heat. White cloth reflects much of the light away. Picking 'the Sun shines harder on black' is a common idea, but the sunlight is the same on both.

flow.context: In this step, you compare a black and a white cloth in the sun.

flow.do: Look at your list. Sort the jobs under: it warms, it feeds, it makes electricity, it fades colour, it helps us see.
flow.say: Let's sort our jobs into groups. Which jobs turn light into heat? Which feed plants? Which make electricity?
flow.kid: Sort your jobs into groups. How many groups do you need?
flow.context: In this step, you sort the jobs of light into groups.

activities.title: From the Sun to an Idli: follow the energy

materials.item: a few sheets of plain paper and crayons or pencils
a handful of raw rice and a handful of urad dal, or pictures of them
scissors and glue

schedule.what: Draw the trail from the Sun to an idli, find a second trail, and talk about where the energy goes.

activities.record: A drawn chain of boxes with arrows from the Sun to an idli, with a short label in every box, and a second chain of your own choice.
activities.safety: Raw rice and dal are for looking only, not for eating, and small children must not put grains in their mouths or noses. If anyone has a food allergy, use pictures instead of the grains.
activities.context: In this activity, you follow the energy in a plate of idli back to sunlight, step by step. You find that most of the energy in your food was sunlight a short while ago.

setup.art: A row of boxes joined by arrows: the Sun, a rice field, a bowl of rice and dal, batter, steaming idlis, a child running.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the chain of boxes from the Sun to the child.

setup.art: A paddy plant with a close-up of a green leaf and arrows labelled sunlight, water and air going in and sugar going out.
setup.caption: 2. Draw what a leaf does with sunlight.

setup.art: A second chain of boxes drawn by the child, for a banana, a glass of milk or a cotton shirt.
setup.caption: 3. Choose something else and follow its energy back to the Sun.

flow.do: Look at the rice and dal. Ask where each came from. Draw the first four boxes on a sheet of paper: Sun, rice and dal plants, grains, batter. Draw arrows between them.
flow.say: An idli is made of rice and dal. Where did they come from? What did the plants need to grow? Let's start at the idli and go backward until we reach the Sun.
flow.kid: Rice and dal came from plants. What did the plants need? Draw the boxes.

ask.q: What does a rice plant take from the sky to make the grains?
good: Sunlight and a gas from the air.

flow.parent: A leaf uses sunlight to join water and carbon dioxide from the air into sugar. This is photosynthesis. The sugar is the plant's stored energy. The sugar ends up in the grain.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sun-to-idli trail. You start at the idli and work backward.

flow.do: Add the last boxes: idli on the plate, you eating, you running. Ask your child to say what changes into what in each arrow. Write it on the arrow.
flow.say: Go forward now. The Sun's light becomes sugar in the leaf. The sugar becomes the grain. The grain becomes the idli. The idli becomes your energy. What does your energy do?
flow.kid: Go forward from the Sun to you. What changes into what on each arrow?
flow.parent: On the last arrows, the energy becomes movement and heat in the child's body. A child's body stays warm because food energy keeps turning into heat. Nothing is lost. The energy only changes form.

check.q: Which is the best way to say where the energy in an idli came from?
options: From sunlight that the rice and dal plants stored
From the steam that cooked it
From the idli plate
From the water in the batter
check.why: Plants catch sunlight and store its energy in their grains. The steam only warms the idli. Picking 'the steam' is a common idea, because cooking feels like adding energy, but the energy we get when we eat comes from the food itself, which was stored from sunlight.

flow.context: In this step, you finish the trail and say what changes into what.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose another thing and follow its energy back. A banana, a glass of milk, or a cotton shirt are good choices. Draw the second chain. For milk, include the grass or fodder that the cow eats.
flow.say: Choose something else. A banana, a glass of milk or a shirt. Where did it come from? What did that need? Keep asking until you reach the Sun.
flow.kid: Pick another thing. A banana or a glass of milk. Follow it back to the Sun.
flow.parent: A glass of milk goes back to the cow, then to the grass or fodder she ate, then to sunlight. A cotton shirt goes back to a cotton plant, then to sunlight. Few things around us do not start from the Sun, so it is good to try a hard one. With 2 to 4 children, each draws a different second chain and the group compares them.
flow.context: In this step, you follow the energy of a second thing back to the Sun.

flow.do: Look at both chains. Ask your child if there is anything in the house whose energy does not come from sunlight. Talk about it.
flow.say: Look at the two chains. Is there anything in our home whose energy did not start with the Sun?
flow.kid: Look at your chains. Does anything in your home not start with the Sun?

ask.q: Can you think of anything whose energy did not come from the Sun?
good: A nuclear power station, which uses energy stored inside atoms.
I could not think of any.

flow.parent: Good answers can include the heat inside the Earth and the energy of atoms in a nuclear power station. Almost everything else leads back to the Sun, including coal, oil, wind, rain and food.
flow.context: In this step, you look for something that does not start from sunlight.

activities.title: Comet Tail Model: a tail that always points away

materials.item: a table fan with a safety guard
a small ball of clay, about the size of a marble
a thin pinch of cotton wool, pulled into a long wisp
a long piece of thread, about 40 centimetres
a pencil or a stick, and some sticky tape

schedule.what: Build the comet, hang it in front of a fan, and move it around the fan to see which way the tail points.

activities.record: Draw the comet in the middle of a page and the fan at four places around it (in front, to the left, to the right, behind). Draw the tail on the comet each time. Write what you notice about the direction of the tail.
activities.safety: Keep fingers, hair and the thread away from the fan blades. Use the lowest speed, keep the guard on, and switch the fan off before you move it.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a model comet and a model Sun, and test which way a comet's tail points as the comet moves around the Sun.

setup.art: A marble-sized clay ball with a wisp of cotton wool stuck to one side, hanging from a thread tied to a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Make the comet. Stick a wisp of cotton wool to a ball of clay and hang it from a thread.

setup.art: A table fan on a table, switched on low, with the cotton wool comet hanging in front of it and the tail streaming away from the fan.
setup.caption: 2. Switch the fan on low. The fan is the Sun. Hold the comet in front of it.

setup.art: A bird's eye view of the comet in the middle and the fan drawn at four places around it, with the tail pointing away from the fan every time.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the comet still and move the fan to its other sides. Then walk the comet toward the fan and away from it. Watch which way the tail points.

flow.do: Roll the clay ball. Press a long wisp of cotton wool onto one side of it. Tie the thread round the clay and tie the other end to a pencil. Ask your child to guess which way the tail will point when the fan is switched on.
flow.say: A comet is a ball of ice and dust. Near the Sun it grows a tail. The fan will be our Sun. When the Sun blows on the comet, which way do you think the tail will point? Why?
flow.kid: Make a comet from clay and cotton wool. Hang it from the thread. Guess where the tail will point.

ask.q: Which way do you think the tail will point? Why?
good: Away from the fan, because the fan pushes it.
Behind the comet as it moves.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think a tail trails behind a moving comet, like the tail of a kite. Real comet tails point away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is moving.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Comet Tail Model. You make the comet and guess before you test.

flow.do: Place the fan on a table and switch it on low. Hold the comet by its thread, 30 centimetres in front of the fan. Watch the tail. A fan blows only forwards. So switch it off and turn it to face the comet from the left. Switch it on and watch. Repeat from the right and from the far side. Last, walk the comet toward the fan, then away. Does the tail trail or lead?
flow.say: Hold the comet in front of the fan. Which way does the tail go? Now move the fan to a different side. Does the tail always point away from the fan? Walk the comet toward the fan and then away. Where is the tail now?
flow.kid: Hold the comet in front of the fan. Watch the tail. Move the fan to other sides of the comet. Walk the comet toward and away from the fan.
flow.parent: The tail streams away from the fan from every side. When the comet walks toward the fan, the tail trails behind it. When it walks away, the tail leads in front, which is how a real comet's tail can lead when it is leaving the Sun. Keep the comet steady so that it does not touch the guard. Switch the fan off before you adjust anything. Use the lowest speed. If the tail hangs limp, use a thinner wisp or a smaller clay ball, or move the comet a little closer to the fan, without touching the guard. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the comet, one moves the fan, one draws and one writes. Swap after each side.

check.q: As the model comet goes round the fan, which way does its tail point?
options: Away from the fan, wherever the comet is
Behind the comet, the way it moves
Toward the fan
Always to the left
check.why: The tail streams in the direction the push is going, which is away from the fan. A real comet's tail points away from the Sun in the same way. Picking 'behind the comet' is a common idea, because a kite's tail trails behind it, but a comet's tail is blown by the Sun, not left behind.

flow.context: In this step, you move the comet around the fan and watch its tail.

flow.do: Talk about what the model gets right and wrong. Read the notes together. Draw a real comet with its tail pointing away from the Sun, at two places on its path.
flow.say: In space, there is no wind from a fan. The Sun pushes the comet's dust and gas with its light, and with a stream of tiny particles. That push is far gentler than a fan. But the direction is the same.
flow.kid: The Sun pushes a comet's tail. Draw a comet in two places, with the tail pointing away from the Sun.
flow.parent: The model shows the direction well. It is not exact. Real comet tails are blown mainly by the stream of particles from the Sun, called the solar wind, and by the push of sunlight on dust. The push of light is tiny, but a comet's dust is so light that it adds up.
flow.context: In this step, you decide what the model gets right and what it gets wrong.

activities.title: Feel the Invisible Warmth: infrared from a warm tumbler

materials.item: a steel tumbler filled to the top with warm water from the tap or a geyser, about 45 degrees (not boiling and not hot enough to hurt)
a second, matching steel tumbler filled with ordinary tap water, as the control
a piece of thick card, about 20 centimetres square
a scarf or cloth to cover the eyes, or just closed eyes
a helper, a grown-up or an older child

schedule.what: Fill the tumbler with warm water, find where it is with eyes closed, then block the warmth with a card.

activities.record: Write how many of the 6 tries you said warm or plain correctly, how many times you pointed to the right side, and what happened when the card was put in the way.
activities.safety: A grown-up fills the tumblers. The water must be warm, not hot. Never use boiling or kettle water. Test it with the back of your hand: you must be able to hold your hand against the tumbler for 5 seconds.
activities.context: In this activity, you find a warm tumbler with your eyes closed, using only the invisible warmth it gives out. You find out that infrared is something your skin can feel.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm water into a steel tumbler, and testing it with the back of their hand.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up fills a tumbler with warm water. Test it with the back of a hand.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed and a helper holding the tumbler 3 centimetres from the child's left cheek, without touching.
setup.caption: 2. With your eyes closed, point to where the tumbler is.

setup.art: The same child with a card held between the tumbler and the cheek, and the child looking puzzled.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a card between the tumbler and your cheek. What happens?

flow.do: A grown-up fills the steel tumbler with warm water. Test it with the back of your hand. Ask your child to guess whether they can tell where the tumbler is with their eyes closed. Write the guess.
flow.say: I will hold a warm tumbler near your face without touching it. Your eyes will be closed. Can you tell where it is? How will you know? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A helper holds a warm tumbler near your face. Can you tell where it is with your eyes closed?

ask.q: How could you tell where it is without seeing or touching it?
good: I will not be able to.

flow.parent: The water must be warm, not hot, in case the tumbler touches the face. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel the Invisible Warmth. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Your child closes their eyes. The helper holds the tumbler about 3 centimetres from the left cheek, without touching. Then the right cheek. Then in front of the nose. Do 6 tries in a mixed order: 3 warm and 3 plain, in a pattern your child cannot guess. Each time, your child says warm or plain, and points to the tumbler. Count how many of 6 are right.
flow.say: Eyes closed. Is the tumbler near your face warm or plain? Point to where you think it is. No touching. Keep still and wait a few seconds. How many did you get right?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Say warm or plain, and point to where it is. Try six times.
flow.parent: Most children get most of them right, because a plain tumbler gives no warmth at all. Guessing by luck would give about 3 of 6, so a score of 5 or 6 is a real sign. Move the tumbler slowly and keep it 2 to 3 centimetres from the skin, with no sound or touch as clues. Warm air rising from the tumbler helps too, so the test does not prove the warmth is only infrared. Part of what the cheek feels is infrared light from the tumbler, landing on the skin. With 2 to 4 children: one is tested, one holds the tumblers, one keeps the score, and they swap.
flow.context: In this step, you find the warm tumbler with your eyes closed.

flow.do: Hold the tumbler near the cheek again. Slide the card between the tumbler and the cheek. Ask your child what changes. Then take the card away and ask what changes again.
flow.say: I'll hold the tumbler where it was. Now I put the card between. What do you feel? Now I take it away. What happens? What did the card block?
flow.kid: Feel the warmth. A card goes in the way. What happens? What does the card block?

check.q: The warmth stopped when a card was put between the tumbler and your cheek. What does that suggest?
options: Something travelled across the gap from the tumbler, and the card stopped it
The tumbler cooled down at that moment
The warmth was in your imagination
The card was cold
check.why: You felt the warmth across a gap, with nothing touching. It stopped when the card blocked the way, and came back when the card moved. That fits infrared light travelling from the tumbler and being stopped by the card. Picking 'the tumbler cooled down' does not fit, because the warmth came back at once when the card moved.

flow.context: In this step, you block the warmth with a card to show that something travels from the tumbler to your cheek.

projects.title: The Grease-Spot Light Meter: which torch is brighter, and by how much?

materials.item: a sheet of plain white paper, A4 size
a few drops of cooking oil and a piece of cotton wool or tissue
a phone with a torch
2 identical small LED key-ring torches
a long table or a long board, at least 1 metre, and a tape measure
modelling clay or a stack of books, to hold the paper upright

projects.safety: Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Keep the cooking oil away from the torches and wipe your hands afterwards. Do not open the key-ring torches: their small button batteries are dangerous if swallowed, so keep them from little children. If anyone has a nut allergy, use coconut or sunflower oil, not groundnut oil.

schedule.what: Make the oil spot paper. Compare the phone torch with one key-ring torch and work out how many times brighter the phone torch is.
Tape the two key-ring torches together and test whether they give twice the light of one.

projects.record: A table with the distance of each torch from the paper when the spot vanished, and the ratio of the squares of the distances. Draw the set-up and write what the spot looked like when it vanished.
projects.context: In this project, you build a light meter from an oil spot on paper, which people used in the 1800s. You use it to find how many times brighter one torch is than another.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper with a round oil spot the size of a coin in the middle, held up to a window so that the spot glows.
setup.caption: 1. Rub a drop of oil on the paper. The spot lets light through.

setup.art: The paper standing upright in the middle of a long table, with a phone torch at one end and a key-ring torch at the other, both aimed at the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the paper in the middle. Put one torch on each side.

setup.art: The same paper from close up, where the oil spot has almost vanished, with a tape measure beside the table showing both distances.
setup.caption: 3. Move one torch until the spot nearly vanishes. Measure both distances.

flow.do: Show your child the two torches. Ask which they think is brighter, and by how many times. Write the guess. Explain that the paper with the oil spot will be the judge.
flow.say: Which torch is brighter, the phone torch or the small key-ring torch? How many times brighter? We will build a meter to find out. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which torch is brighter, the phone or the key-ring torch? How many times brighter? Why?

ask.q: How could you tell exactly how many times brighter one torch is?
good: Count how far away I need to put each torch to make them match.
Compare the patches they make on a wall.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often guess that the phone torch is about twice as bright, and are surprised by the answer. A strong phone torch is often many times brighter than a key-ring torch.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Grease-Spot Light Meter project. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Draw a circle the size of a coin in the middle of the paper with a pencil. Rub a few drops of cooking oil over it with cotton wool. Wait 2 minutes. Blot off extra oil. Hold the paper up to a window. The spot should glow more than the rest. Stand the paper upright in the middle of the table, held in clay.
flow.say: The oil makes the paper thinner for light. More light can pass through the spot. Hold it up to the window. Does the spot look different from the rest of the paper?
flow.kid: Rub oil on a coin-sized circle. Hold it to the window. The spot looks different.
flow.parent: If the spot is not clear, use a little more oil. Blot well, so that no oil runs. Mark the middle of the table. The paper stands there with the oil spot facing along the table.
flow.context: In this step, you make the oil spot paper that will be your light meter.

flow.do: Make the room dark. Put the phone torch 50 centimetres from the paper, on one side, pointing at it. Put the key-ring torch on the other side, close to the paper. Look at the paper from beside the phone torch. Slide the key-ring torch away slowly until the spot almost vanishes. Measure both distances.
flow.say: Look at the spot. Is it darker or brighter than the paper around it? Slide the small torch slowly. When the spot vanishes, both sides are getting the same light. Stop and measure.
flow.kid: Slide the small torch away slowly. Stop when the spot almost vanishes. Measure both distances.
flow.parent: The spot looks dark when the near side is brighter, and bright when the far side is brighter. It nearly vanishes when the two sides get equal light. Look from one side, a little off the line of the torches, so you do not block the light. Take your time. The point of vanishing is a range of a few centimetres, so choose the middle. Repeat twice. The room must be properly dark, or the spot will never vanish. The rule works best when the torches are not too close, so if the key-ring torch ends up nearer than about 10 centimetres, move the phone torch further away (up to 80 centimetres) and start again. Real ratios vary a lot, from about 3 to 20 times, depending on the torches. With 2 to 4 children: one slides the key-ring torch, one watches the spot from the side, one measures and one writes. One child alone: tape the phone torch down and slide the key-ring torch yourself.
flow.context: In this step, you find where the two torches give the same light, using the spot as the judge.

flow.do: Write the two distances. Work out each one multiplied by itself. Divide the bigger by the smaller. This is how many times brighter the phone torch is.
flow.say: Light thins out with the square of the distance. So we multiply each distance by itself. Then we divide. For example, if the phone is at 50 and the key-ring is at 20, then 2500 divided by 400 is about 6.
flow.kid: Multiply each distance by itself. Divide the bigger by the smaller. That is how many times brighter.

check.q: The phone torch is 50 centimetres from the paper, and the key-ring torch is 25 centimetres away when the spot vanishes. How many times brighter is the phone torch?
options: 4 times brighter
2 times brighter
The same brightness
8 times brighter
check.why: The phone torch is twice as far away, but gives the same light on the paper. Twice as far spreads the light over four times the area, so the phone torch must be four times as bright to match. Picking 2 is the common slip, because the distances differ by two times. The brightness differs by the square of that.

flow.context: In this step, you turn the two distances into a number: how many times brighter one torch is.

flow.do: On day 2, tape the two key-ring torches together so that they point the same way. Repeat the test with the phone torch fixed at 50 centimetres. Find the new distance where the spot vanishes. Work out how many times brighter than one key-ring torch the pair is.
flow.say: Now two torches give light on one side. Should the spot vanish at a different distance? Do the sum again. Is the pair about twice as bright as one?
flow.kid: Tape the two small torches together. Find the new place where the spot vanishes. Do the sum again.
flow.parent: The pair should balance at about 1.4 times the distance of a single torch, because 1.4 times 1.4 is about 2. That means the pair is about twice as bright. Real results will be rough. If your answer is between 1.5 and 2.5, the meter is working.
flow.context: In this step, you test your meter. Two torches taped together should give about twice the light of one.

challenges.title: Ice Challenge: melt one cube first, and keep another one longest
challenges.problem: You have two ice cubes of the same size and 30 minutes of sunshine. Using only things from the kitchen, make one cube melt as fast as you can, and keep the other cube from melting for as long as you can.
constraints: The two cubes must start the same size and sit in the same sunshine.
You may use paper, cloth, foil, cups, jars, plates and cardboard. You may not use any heater, stove or hot water.
You may not touch the cubes after you start the timer.
Stop at 30 minutes, or when the first cube is gone.
materials: 2 ice cubes of the same size
black paper or cloth, white paper, aluminium foil, thin card
a clear glass jar or a clear plastic box
general: Put one cube on black paper, and the other on white paper, in the sun.
Cover the cube you want to keep with a foil dome that has no gap, with the shiny side out.
Put the cube you want to melt first in a clear jar on black paper, so that heat stays in.
creative: Make a small tent of foil over the cube you want to keep, and put white paper under it, so that very little light is absorbed.
Make a cone of foil round the cube you want to melt, to bounce extra sunlight onto it.
Stand the cube you want to keep inside a plastic cup, inside a bigger cup with a gap of air between, and cover with foil.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your two designs. Build them and start the timer together. Which cube melted first and which lasted longest? What worked best, and what would you change? Try again with one change.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about light and heat. You use what you know about reflecting and absorbing light to melt one ice cube and save another.

setup.art: A child sketching two designs on paper: a cube on black paper in a jar, and a cube under a foil dome.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch your two designs.

setup.art: Two ice cubes in the sun, one in a clear jar on black paper and one under a shiny foil dome, with a phone timer between them.
setup.caption: 2. Build both, set them in the same sunshine and start the timer.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two designs, one to melt and one to keep. Ask what they know about black, white and shiny things in the sun.
flow.say: You want one cube to melt fast and one to last. What did black paper do in the Ice Race? What does a shiny sheet of foil do with sunlight? Sketch your ideas first.
flow.kid: One cube melts fast. One lasts long. Draw your ideas first.

ask.q: What would make a cube melt faster?
good: Keeping the heat in with a jar.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Ice Challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build the two designs. Take the ice cubes out of the freezer only when you are ready. Put both set-ups in the same sunshine and start the timer. Look every 5 minutes.
flow.say: Build both designs. Take the ice out last. Start the timer at the same moment. Check every 5 minutes. Which cube is melting faster?
flow.kid: Build your two designs. Put both in the sun. Start the timer. Check every 5 minutes.
flow.parent: Keep the foil edges folded over so they are not sharp. Foil in the sun can throw a bright reflection into eyes, so keep it low and pointed away from people. A sunny spot is needed. If the sun is weak, the difference may be small.
flow.context: In this step, you build the two designs and start the race.

flow.do: At 30 minutes, or when the first cube is gone, stop. Compare the two cubes. Write down what worked and what did not. Make one change and try again if there is time.
flow.say: Which cube melted first? Which lasted longest? Why do you think your design did that? What is one change you would try next?
flow.kid: Which cube melted first? Which lasted longest? What would you change?

check.q: A shiny foil dome helped to keep a cube from melting in the sun. Why?
options: It reflected most of the sunlight, so little was turned into heat
It made its own cold
It took in the sunlight and kept it
It blocked the air
check.why: Shiny foil reflects most of the light that lands on it, so little of the sunlight becomes heat. Picking 'it took in the sunlight' is the opposite. That is what black paper does.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your two designs and say why they worked.

challenges.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Shiny foil can throw a bright reflection into eyes, so keep it low and point it away from people. Fold the foil edges over, because cut foil can be sharp.

challenges.title: Power Cut Reading: light a page with one small torch
challenges.problem: It is a power cut and you have one small torch, one page of a book, and a room with white walls. Place the torch and anything else you can find so that the page is as bright as possible, from a torch kept at least 50 centimetres away.
constraints: You may use only one torch.
The torch must be at least 50 centimetres from the page.
You may use anything from the home that is not electric.
Judge the brightness by how easy it is to read the small print.
materials: one small torch or a phone torch
a book with a page of small print
aluminium foil, white paper, a steel plate or tray
a steel tumbler or a glass jar
general: Bring the torch closer to the page. Light thins out with distance, so closer is brighter.
Point the torch at a white wall or ceiling, and let the wall's light fall on the page.
Stand the torch inside a clear jar or tumbler on its side so the light spreads over the page.
creative: Put crumpled foil, shiny side out, behind the torch to bounce more light forward.
Make a cone of white card round the torch to keep light from spreading sideways.
Place a steel plate beside the page, so that it bounces torchlight back onto the print.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your plan. Build it and test it by reading the same line of print. Which plan made the print easiest to read? Why do you think it worked?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about light thinning out. You find ways to make a small torch light a page better, without moving it closer.

setup.art: A child sketching a torch, a book and a wall in a dark room, with arrows for light going from the torch to the wall and from the wall to the page.
