flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to sketch two plans. Ask what happens to light as it travels from the torch to the page.
flow.say: A small torch 50 centimetres away makes a dim page. Light spreads out as it travels. How could you stop it from spreading so much, or collect more of it? Draw two ideas.
flow.kid: A small torch. A dim page. Draw two ideas to make the page brighter.

ask.q: What happens to the torch's light by the time it reaches the page?
good: Most of it missed the page.

flow.context: This is the first step of Power Cut Reading. You plan.

flow.do: Build the first plan and test it. Read the same line of small print. Rate it from 1 to 5 for how easy it is to read. Then build the second plan and rate it.
flow.say: Test your first plan. Can you read the small print? How easy is it, from 1 to 5? Now the second plan.
flow.kid: Test plan one. Rate it from 1 to 5. Test plan two. Rate it.
flow.parent: Keep the room as dark as possible. Let your eyes get used to the dark for a minute. Use the same line of print each time. If both plans are about equal, try one thing from the lists of ideas.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test your two plans.

flow.do: Compare the plans. Talk about why the best one worked. Try to improve it with one more change.
flow.say: Which plan was best? Where did the extra light on the page come from? What would you change next?
flow.kid: Which plan was best? Why? What would you change?

check.q: A white wall behind the torch made the page easier to read. Why?
options: The wall bounced light that would otherwise have been lost onto the page
The wall made its own light
The wall made the torch brighter
The wall pulled the light toward it
check.why: A white wall reflects most of the light that lands on it. Some of that light travels on to the page, adding to the torch's own light. Picking 'the wall made its own light' mixes up reflecting light with making light.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your plans and explain which worked best.

challenges.safety: Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Do the test with a grown-up nearby, in a room with no candles or flames.

worksheets.title: Light Spreads, Warms and Has a Family (core)

items.p: A lamp lights a page 1 metre away. The page is moved to 2 metres away. What happens to the light that falls on one square centimetre of the page?
opts: It becomes one quarter as much
items.why: At twice the distance, the same light covers four times the area. So each square centimetre gets one quarter as much. Picking half is the common guess, because the distance doubled. The patch grows in two directions, wide and tall, so the area grows four times.

items.p: A star far away looks dim because its light gets used up on the journey through empty space. True or false?
items.why: False. In empty space, light is not used up. It spreads over a bigger and bigger area, so the light that reaches your eye is thin. A strong answer says the energy is not lost, only shared out.

items.p: If you go three times as far from a lamp, the same light covers ____ times the area.
items.why: Three times as far makes the patch three times as wide and three times as tall. Three times three is nine. So each part of the patch gets one ninth as much light.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does with most of the light that lands on it.
pairs: lets most of the light through
reflects most of the light and absorbs some
items.why: A surface can reflect light, absorb it or let it through, and most do a mix. The three parts always add up to all the light that landed.

items.p: A school bag left in the sun feels hotter when it is black than when it is white. What is the best reason?
opts: Black takes in more of the sunlight and turns it into heat
The Sun shines harder on black things
items.why: The sunlight is the same for both bags. Black absorbs most of it, so the energy of the light becomes heat. White reflects much of it away. Picking 'the Sun shines harder' is a common idea, but the sunlight on the two bags is the same.

items.p: Sort these. Does it mostly reflect sunlight or mostly absorb it?
items.why: Light colours and shiny surfaces send most sunlight back, so they stay cooler. Dark surfaces take it in and turn it to heat, so they warm up fast.

items.p: When a black road absorbs sunlight, the energy of the light is destroyed. True or false?
items.why: False. Energy is never destroyed. When the road absorbs sunlight, the energy turns into heat, and the road gets warmer. A strong answer says where the energy went.

items.p: Kavya says, 'The street light at the end of our road is dim, so it must be a weak lamp.' Another lamp of the same kind, right outside her window, looks very bright. What would you tell Kavya?
items.a: The two lamps could be the same. The far lamp's light has spread over a much bigger area by the time it reaches Kavya, so each part of her eye gets less. Brightness depends on distance as well as on the lamp.
items.why: A strong answer says the lamp is not weaker, and gives distance and spreading as the reason.

items.p: Which member of the light family can our eyes see?
items.why: Our eyes catch only visible light, from violet to red. Infrared, radio waves and X-rays are real, but our eyes cannot see them.

items.p: Put these members of the light family in order, from the longest wavelength to the shortest.
items.why: The family runs from radio waves, as long as a room, down to X-rays, as short as an atom. Visible light sits in the middle, closer to the short end.

items.p: The invisible light that a TV remote sends out is called ____.
items.why: Infrared is light just beyond red. The remote sends a pattern of flickers of it, and the TV reads the pattern.

items.p: Draw a torch, a card with a small square hole in it, and a wall. Show the light spreading after the hole. Then show how the patch on a wall twice as far away would look.
items.a: A torch on the left, the card in the middle, and two walls on the right, one near and one far. Straight lines spread out from the hole. The patch on the far wall is much bigger, about four times the area, and fainter.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lines spreading out in a cone and the far patch covering more area with less light on each part.
items.art: A torch on a table on the left and a blank wall on the right, with an empty card standing between them.

items.p: In 1800, William Herschel found that a thermometer placed just past the red end of the colours got warm. What did this show?
opts: Sunlight has rays that our eyes cannot see
Red light is hotter than the Sun
items.why: Nothing could be seen in that spot, yet the thermometer warmed. So something unseen, now called infrared, was arriving from the Sun. Picking 'the thermometer was broken' is the first thing many people think. Herschel's controls in the shade did not warm, so it was not the room.

items.p: Three children look at the dark patch just beyond the red end of a rainbow made by a prism. Each says something different.

views.says: Dark means there is no light there. Nothing can warm a thermometer in a dark place.
There may be rays there that our eyes cannot see, and the thermometer can feel them.
We cannot tell by looking. We would have to test it with an instrument.

items.ask: Which view fits best with what Herschel found? Say why, and say one thing another child gets right.
items.a: Arjun's view fits, since Herschel's thermometer warmed in the dark patch. The aunt is right that we need an instrument, which is what Herschel used. Meenakshi's idea was what most people thought, because dark seems to mean no light.
items.why: A strong answer picks one view with evidence from the thermometer and credits a point from another.

items.p: Radio waves and X-rays are the same kind of wave as visible light, only with a different wavelength. True or false?
items.why: True. All the members of the family are waves of electric and magnetic fields that travel at the speed of light in empty space. They differ in wavelength, and so in the energy of each photon.

items.p: A torch makes a lit square patch 5 squares wide and 5 squares tall when the paper is 20 centimetres away. How many squares would the patch cover at 40 centimetres?
items.why: At twice the distance the patch is twice as wide and twice as tall. That is 10 squares by 10 squares, which is 100. Or, 25 times 4 is 100.

worksheets.title: Energy, Waves and the Push of Light (stretch)

items.p: Jupiter is about 5 times further from the Sun than the Earth is. About how much sunlight does a square metre of Jupiter's cloud tops get, compared with a square metre on Earth?
items.why: Five times as far means the light is spread over 5 times 5, which is 25 times the area. So each square metre gets about one twenty-fifth as much. Picking one fifth is the common slip, as it forgets that the area grows in two directions.

items.p: A torch beam makes a patch of exactly the same brightness on a wall 1 metre away and on a wall 3 metres away. True or false?
items.why: False. At 3 metres, the light covers 9 times the area, so the patch is much dimmer. The total light from the torch is the same. It is just spread more thinly.

items.p: To make the light on a patch 16 times thinner, you move ____ times as far from the lamp.
items.why: Four times as far gives 4 times 4, which is 16 times the area. The same light is shared by 16 times as much area, so each part gets one sixteenth.

items.p: Priya paints her flat's roof white. Her neighbour's roof is black tar. Which flat will be cooler in May, and why? Use the words reflect and absorb.
items.a: Priya's flat will be cooler. The white roof reflects most of the sunlight, so little of it turns into heat. The black tar roof absorbs most of the sunlight, and the light's energy becomes heat, so the roof and the flat below get hot.
items.why: A strong answer says white reflects, black absorbs, and absorbed light turns into heat.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found out.
pairs: found invisible heating rays beyond the red end of the colours
found invisible rays beyond the violet end of the colours
made radio waves in a lab and showed they act like light
measured the tiny push that light gives
items.why: Each person added a piece to the picture of the light family. Together they show that the light we see is a thin slice of a long family of waves.

items.p: Sort these. Is the wave longer than visible light, or shorter?
items: the infrared from a TV remote
gamma rays from an exploding star
items.why: The family runs from radio, the longest, through microwaves and infrared, then visible light, then ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, the shortest.

items.p: A pit viper hunts a warm mouse in total darkness. What does the snake sense?
opts: The infrared that the warm mouse gives out
A sound too high for us to hear
items.why: All warm things give out infrared, and pit vipers have small pits on their faces that sense it. Picking 'light made by the snake' mixes up sensing light with making light.

items.p: A comet's tail trails behind it as the comet moves, the way a kite's tail trails behind a kite. True or false?
items.why: False. A comet's tail points away from the Sun, even when the comet is moving toward the Sun or away from it. The Sun's light and the stream of particles from the Sun push the tail outward.

items.p: Put these in order of the energy each photon carries, from the least to the most.
items.why: The shorter the wavelength, the more energy each photon carries. Radio photons carry very little, and X-ray photons carry thousands of times more than visible light photons.

items.p: Explain in your own words why a thermometer in a dark patch just past the red end of the colours got warm. Use the word energy.
items.a: Invisible rays from the Sun, which we now call infrared, fell on the thermometer's black bulb. The bulb absorbed them, and their energy turned into heat. So the thermometer warmed even though no light could be seen.
items.why: A strong answer says something unseen carried energy to the thermometer and that absorbed energy becomes heat.

items.p: The Earth stays at a fairly steady temperature over the years. What is the best reason?
opts: It gives out as much infrared as it takes in as sunlight
It makes no heat of its own
It stores all the sunlight forever
items.why: If the Earth took in more energy than it gave out, it would keep heating up. It settles at the temperature where the infrared going out matches the sunlight coming in. Gases such as carbon dioxide slow the way out, which is why adding more of them warms the Earth.

items.p: Draw the light family as a long ribbon. Mark where radio waves, visible light and gamma rays go. Colour in the thin slice that your eyes can see.
items.a: A long ribbon, with radio waves at the left end, then microwaves, infrared, a small rainbow slice for visible light, then ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays at the right end. The visible slice is very small.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the family in order of wavelength, with the visible slice small and in the middle, nearer the short end.
items.art: An empty long ribbon with a small tick mark in the middle.

items.p: A lamp gives a page 36 units of light when the page is 2 metres away. How many units does the page get at 6 metres?
items.why: 6 metres is 3 times as far as 2 metres. Three times as far means 3 times 3, which is 9 times the area. 36 divided by 9 is 4.

items.p: A Crookes radiometer is a glass bulb with a little air inside and a set of vanes that spin in sunlight. A child asks what makes it spin.

views.says: The light pushes the vanes directly, a little like wind pushing a windmill.
The black sides get warm, and the air right next to them moves and pushes the vanes.
It must be something to do with the glass. Light cannot push anything.

items.ask: The radiometer spins best with a little air left inside, and almost stops in a very good vacuum. Which view fits that evidence best, and why?
items.a: The second view fits best. If light pushed the vanes, the spinning would be stronger in a better vacuum, but it stops. The air is needed. The sceptic is wrong that light cannot push, as it can, only far too weakly to turn the vanes.
items.why: A strong answer uses the vacuum evidence to prefer the gas view and says the push of light is real but tiny.

items.p: The tiny push that light gives to anything it lands on is called radiation ____.
items.why: Radiation pressure is real, but very small. Sunlight pushing on a square metre of shiny sheet gives about the weight of one grain of sugar.

items.p: Three of these are members of the light family. Which one is NOT?
items.why: Sound is a vibration of air, water or solids, and needs something to travel through. The other three are waves of electric and magnetic fields, which cross empty space.

items.p: A shiny foil dome can keep an ice cube from melting in the sun, because the foil reflects most of the sunlight. True or false?
items.why: True. Shiny foil sends most of the sunlight back, so little of it turns into heat. A black cover would do the opposite.

items.p: Radio telescopes find a faint glow of microwaves coming from every direction in the sky. What is the best explanation?
opts: It is the oldest light there is, from the young universe, stretched into microwaves
It is heat from the Sun
It is light from a nearby lamp
items.why: The glow is the same from every direction, which fits light that was set free when the whole universe was young. As space grew, the waves were stretched until they became microwaves. Scientists agree the glow is real. They argue about what it says of the start.

items.p: Two identical torches taped together light a page with a certain amount of light. If you move the pair twice as far from the page, the page gets the same light as one torch gave at the start. True or false?
items.why: False. Two torches give twice the light, but at twice the distance the light is four times thinner. Two divided by four is a half. The page gets only half of what one torch gave at the start.

items.p: To light a page equally from twice as far away, you need ____ times as many torches.
items.why: At twice the distance, each torch gives one quarter as much light. So you need four times as many torches to make up the difference.

items.p: Match each instrument to the part of the light family it catches.
pairs: ultraviolet, which it helps to block
items.why: Different tools are built for different members of the family. Each one reveals something our eyes cannot see.

items.p: Sort these. When light lands on it, does the light mostly become heat, mostly bounce back, or mostly go through?
items.why: What a surface does with light depends on what it is made of and how smooth it is. The three outcomes always add up to all the light that landed.

items.p: Explain to a younger child why all the food in the world starts with sunlight. Use a plate of idli or rice as your example.
items.a: Rice plants catch sunlight with their leaves and use the energy of the light to make sugar from water and air. The sugar is stored in the grains. When we eat rice, we get that stored energy. So the energy in rice was sunlight a short while ago.
items.why: A strong answer follows the chain from the Sun to the leaf to the grain to the child.

items.p: What gives a solar sail its push?
opts: A rocket hidden in the mast
items.why: Light carries a small push. On a huge, thin, shiny sail, in space with no friction, the push adds up over weeks and months. There is no air in space to blow the sail.

items.p: Draw what happens to a beam of sunlight that lands on black paper, on white paper and on shiny foil. Use arrows to show the light that bounces and the light that is absorbed.
items.a: Three beams arrive at three sheets. Black has an arrow in and almost nothing out, with wavy heat lines rising. White has an arrow in and a big arrow out, with a few heat lines. Foil has an arrow in and nearly the same arrow out, with almost no heat lines.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that what does not bounce is absorbed and becomes heat.
items.art: Three squares labelled black, white and foil with a sunbeam arriving at each.

items.p: In 1967, Jocelyn Bell, a research student, spotted a strange regular signal on a long paper chart from a radio telescope. It turned out to be the first pulsar. Her supervisor, Antony Hewish, shared a Nobel Prize for the discovery in 1974, and she was not part of the prize.

views.says: I noticed the signal and refused to ignore it, so the discovery was mine.

views.who: The prize committee's view, as reported
views.says: The supervisor planned the telescope and led the research, so the prize goes to the leader.
Everyone who built the telescope, checked the signal and worked out what it meant shares the credit.

items.ask: Who should get the credit when a team makes a discovery? Choose a view, give a reason, and say one thing another view gets right.
items.a: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives a clear reason, such as noticing something that others would have missed deserves credit, and then admits that building the telescope and leading the team also mattered.
items.why: This is a question of fairness. A strong answer weighs noticing, leading and building, and does not just repeat the prize.

items.p: FM radio waves are about 3 metres long. How many such waves would fit end to end along 30 metres?
items.why: 30 divided by 3 is 10. About 10 radio waves would fit along 30 metres.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to follow the energy of the Sun into a child who runs after eating idli.
items: Sunlight lands on a rice leaf
The leaf makes sugar from water and air
The child's muscles use the energy to run
items.why: The energy moves from sunlight to sugar in the leaf, to the grain, to the child's body, and then to movement and heat.

items.p: A clear glass jar over a piece of black paper in the sun melts an ice cube faster than black paper on its own. What is the best reason?
opts: The jar lets light in but slows the escape of heat
items.why: Sunlight passes through the clear jar and is absorbed by the black paper. The jar traps the warm air, so heat leaves more slowly. A car left in the sun does the same. Picking 'the jar makes extra light' mixes up trapping light with making light.

items.p: A dark-coloured roof paint can sometimes stay cooler in the sun than a white paint, if it reflects infrared well. True or false?
items.why: True. Colour tells us only about visible light. Sunlight also carries infrared, which we cannot see. Special 'cool roof' paints reflect infrared, so even dark ones stay cooler, and some white paints absorb a lot of infrared.

items.p: A friend says, 'Radio waves and visible light are completely different things.' Explain what they have in common and how they differ.
items.a: Both are the same kind of wave, a wave of electric and magnetic fields. Both travel at the speed of light in empty space. They differ in wavelength. Radio waves are metres long and our eyes cannot see them, while visible light is a tiny fraction of a millimetre and our eyes can see it.
items.why: A strong answer names what they share (kind of wave, speed) and what differs (wavelength, whether we can see it).

items.p: Here is a drawing of Herschel's test. Label the four parts: the prism, the band of colours, the thermometer that warmed most and the control thermometer in the shade.
labels: thermometer just past the red edge
a: prism: the glass block that spreads the sunlight
band of colours: the spread-out sunlight, red at one end and violet at the other
thermometer just past the red edge: it warmed the most
control thermometer in the shade: it shows what the room does by itself
items.why: The control tells you whether a change comes from the room or from the colours. Without it, the surprising warm reading could not be trusted.
items.art: A drawing of a table with a glass prism, a band of colours on the table, three thermometers and four empty label boxes.

quiz.p: You move a torch three times further from a wall. How does the light on each part of the lit patch change?
quiz.why: Three times as far makes the patch 3 times wider and 3 times taller, so 9 times the area. The same light is shared by 9 times as much area. Picking 3 times thinner is the common slip, as it forgets the second direction.

quiz.p: Which sentence about light and distance is true?
opts: Light spreads out, so each patch gets less the further you go
Light gets used up in empty space as it travels
Light stays equally bright however far it goes
Light only spreads out in air
quiz.why: Light spreads over a bigger area as it goes. In clear space none of it is used up. Picking 'used up' is a common idea, because far things look dim, but starlight arrives with its energy intact.

quiz.p: Which roof would keep the rooms below it coolest in a hot summer?
opts: A roof covered with dark tar
A roof covered in dark blue tiles
quiz.why: White reflects most of the sunlight, so little becomes heat. The dark roofs absorb most of the sunlight, which turns into heat that warms the rooms below.

quiz.p: Herschel painted the bulbs of his thermometers black. Why?
opts: Black takes in more of the light, so the thermometer shows the warmth more clearly
Black stops heat from getting in
Black makes the numbers easier to read
quiz.why: A black bulb absorbs most of the rays that land on it and turns them into heat. A clear bulb would let much of the energy pass through, and show a smaller change.

quiz.p: A scientist keeps one thermometer in the shade while testing others in the sun. What is the shaded thermometer for?
opts: To show what happens when nothing special is done
To make the test look neat
quiz.why: A control is left alone so that you can compare. If the control warms too, then the room is warming, and the other readings cannot be trusted by themselves. Picking 'to cool the others' is wrong, because a thermometer cannot cool another from a distance.

quiz.p: Which members of the light family have the longest waves?
quiz.why: From longest to shortest the order is radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. FM radio waves are about 3 metres long. X-rays are as short as an atom.

quiz.p: What do radio waves, visible light and X-rays have in common?
opts: They are all waves of electric and magnetic fields that travel at the speed of light in empty space
They are all made of sound
They all have the same wavelength
quiz.why: They are one family, the electromagnetic spectrum. They differ in wavelength but are the same kind of wave. Picking 'the same wavelength' is the opposite of the truth. The wavelength is exactly what sets them apart.

quiz.p: Why can our eyes not see infrared?
opts: The light-catching cells in our eyes respond only to a thin slice of wavelengths
Infrared is too bright for our eyes
quiz.why: Our eyes are built to catch wavelengths from about 0.0004 to 0.0007 millimetres. Infrared is a little longer, and our eye cells do not respond to it. It is a real member of the light family, and a phone camera can catch it.

quiz.p: Which carries more energy in each photon, ultraviolet or infrared?
opts: It depends on the colour of the sky
quiz.why: The shorter the wavelength, the more energy each photon carries. Ultraviolet is shorter than visible light, and infrared is longer. That is why ultraviolet can burn skin, and infrared only warms it.

quiz.p: Why does the tail of a comet point away from the Sun?
opts: Sunlight and the stream of particles from the Sun push the dust and gas outward
The comet is falling into the Sun
The tail is left behind as the comet moves
The Sun's gravity pulls the tail
quiz.why: Light carries a small push, and the Sun also sends out a stream of particles. Together these push the comet's dust and gas away from the Sun. Picking 'left behind' is a common idea, because a kite's tail trails behind it.

quiz.p: How is the energy in a rice grain connected to the Sun?
opts: The rice plant caught sunlight and stored the energy in the grain
The grain was warmed by the Sun while drying
The grain makes its own energy from nothing
The soil gives the grain its energy
quiz.why: Plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and air, and store the energy in their grains. Warming in the Sun does not add the energy we get from food.

quiz.p: Gases such as carbon dioxide in the air slow the escape of infrared from the Earth. What happens to the Earth's temperature when there is more of them?
opts: The Earth gets brighter at night
quiz.why: The Earth settles where the energy going out equals the energy coming in. If the gases slow the way out, the Earth must get warmer before the balance is reached again.

applications: Solar water heaters on rooftops turn sunlight into heat for baths and kitchens.
Solar panels turn light into electricity for homes, farms, lamps and water pumps.
White roof paint and lime-washed walls reflect sunlight and keep rooms cooler.
Thermal cameras show warm bodies in the dark and spot fevers at airports.
TV, air conditioner and set-top box remotes send invisible infrared signals.
Radio, TV, mobile phones and Wi-Fi all use long waves from the light family.
Hospitals use X-rays to see bones and carefully aimed beams to treat some illnesses.
Sunscreen, hats and umbrellas protect skin from ultraviolet light.
Radio telescopes such as the GMRT near Pune listen to waves from far galaxies.
Solar sails may one day move spacecraft with the push of sunlight and no fuel.

open_questions.q: What happened before the oldest light in the sky was set free?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest light shows us the universe about 380,000 years after it began. Before that, the universe was too hot and dense for light to travel, so we cannot see further back with light.

open_questions.q: Why is the glow of the oldest light so smooth in every direction?
open_questions.why_open: Inflation, a very fast early growth, is the favourite explanation. It has not been proved, and some scientists suggest other ideas.

open_questions.q: Could a fleet of tiny sail craft pushed by lasers really reach another star?
open_questions.why_open: The idea is built on a real push of light, but the engineering is very hard. Nobody has tested a craft at that scale.

open_questions.q: Is there light we cannot yet detect, or waves of another kind that we have not found?
open_questions.why_open: Every few decades, scientists have found new ways to see. Nobody can be sure there is nothing left to find.

open_questions.q: What does it feel like to a pit viper or a bee to sense a slice of the family that we cannot?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what animals respond to, but nobody knows what their experience is like from inside.

open_questions.q: Why do the amounts of energy come in packets, called photons, at all?
open_questions.why_open: Quantum physics predicts how photons behave very well. Why light is built this way is still argued about.

maths.problem: A torch patch is 3 squares wide and 3 squares tall when the paper is 10 centimetres away. The paper moves to 30 centimetres, three times as far. How many squares does the patch cover now, and how many times as many as before?
maths.answer: 81 squares, which is 9 times as many.
maths.explain: At 3 times the distance, the patch is 3 times wider and 3 times taller. That is 9 squares by 9 squares. 9 times 9 is 81. At first it was 3 times 3, which is 9. 81 divided by 9 is 9. So the patch covers 9 times as many squares.
maths.context: In the Torch Spread test, you counted the lit squares at different distances. Here is a pattern to check by multiplying.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the width by the height gives the area, so you can predict the lit squares before you measure them.

maths.problem: One lantern gives 144 units of light at 1 step. At 4 steps, the light is spread over 4 times 4 times the area. How many units does the lantern give at 4 steps?
maths.explain: 4 times 4 is 16. The same 144 units are shared by 16 times the area. 144 divided by 16 is 9. Check: 9 times 16 is 144.
maths.context: In the game Lantern Stalls, you found how much light one lantern gives at each distance. Here is one entry of the table, worked out.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the light by the area tells you how much reaches each part, which is how you work out how many lanterns a far stall needs.

maths.problem: In an Ice Race, the cube on black paper melted in 12 minutes, and the cube on white paper melted in 30 minutes. The cube on white paper lasted how many minutes longer, and about how many times as long?
maths.answer: 18 minutes longer, and about 2 and a half times as long.
maths.explain: 30 take away 12 is 18. For the times: 12 times 2 is 24, and 12 times 2 and a half is 30. So white lasted 2 and a half times as long as black. A made-up example. Your own numbers will differ.
maths.context: In the Ice Race, you timed how long each ice cube lasted on different colours of paper. Here are some made-up times.
maths.why_maths: Comparing times as a ratio shows how much difference the colour made, not just which was first.

maths.problem: Jupiter is about 5 times further from the Sun than the Earth is. Saturn is about 10 times further. How many times thinner is sunlight on Jupiter, and how many times thinner on Saturn, compared with the Earth?
maths.answer: About 25 times thinner on Jupiter, and about 100 times thinner on Saturn.
maths.explain: Light thins by the square of the distance. For Jupiter, 5 times 5 is 25. For Saturn, 10 times 10 is 100. So sunlight on Saturn is about 100 times thinner than on Earth.
maths.context: You found that light covers four times the area at double the distance. Here is the same rule applied to the planets.
maths.why_maths: Squaring the distance turns a distance into a thinning, so a table of distances becomes a table of brightness.

maths.problem: The sunlight that falls on the Earth in one hour holds about as much energy as all of humanity uses in a year. There are 24 hours in a day and 365 days in a year. About how many times more energy does the Sun send to the Earth in a year than humanity uses?
maths.explain: 24 times 365 is 24 times 300, which is 7,200, plus 24 times 65, which is 1,560. 7,200 plus 1,560 is 8,760. So one year holds 8,760 hours. Each hour matches one year of use. So the Sun sends about 8,760 times as much as we use.
maths.context: You followed the Sun's energy into an idli. Here is how much sunlight the Earth gets in all.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying hours in a day by days in a year turns one hour of sunlight into a whole year of it.

maths.problem: About 100 red light waves fit across the width of a hair. A hair is about 0.07 millimetres wide. About how wide is one red light wave in millimetres?
maths.explain: Divide the width of the hair by 100. 0.07 divided by 100 is 0.0007. Dividing by 100 moves the digits two places to the right. So one red wave is about 0.0007 millimetres.
maths.context: You met the light family and its wavelengths. Here is how small a wave of red light is.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by 100 gives the size of one wave from the size of a hair, which shows how tiny visible light is.

maths.problem: In the Grease-Spot Light Meter, the phone torch was 50 centimetres from the paper and the key-ring torch was 20 centimetres away when the spot vanished. About how many times brighter is the phone torch?
maths.explain: Multiply each distance by itself. 50 times 50 is 2,500. 20 times 20 is 400. 2,500 divided by 400 is 6 and a quarter, so about 6 times brighter.
maths.context: In the Grease-Spot Light Meter, you balanced two torches around an oil spot. Here is a sample set of measurements.
maths.why_maths: Squaring both distances and dividing turns two distances into a brightness ratio, so you can compare any two lamps.

maths.problem: Imagine a white wall reflects 8 out of every 10 parts of the sunlight that land on it, and absorbs the rest. If 500 units of sunlight land on the wall, how many units become heat? These numbers are made up.
maths.explain: 8 out of 10 are reflected, so 2 out of 10 are absorbed. 2 tenths of 500 is 500 divided by 10, which is 50, times 2, which is 100. So 100 units become heat. A black wall might absorb 9 out of 10, which is 450 units.
maths.context: You found that surfaces reflect some light and absorb the rest. Here is a made-up example to work out how much heat a wall gets.
maths.why_maths: Taking a fraction of the light shows how much energy turns into heat, so you can compare walls and roofs.

maths.problem: You tape two key-ring torches together. Each gives 1 unit of light at a certain distance. At twice that distance, the light is spread over 4 times the area. How many units does the pair give at twice the distance?
maths.explain: Two torches give 2 units. At twice the distance, the light is 4 times thinner. 2 divided by 4 is one half. So the pair at twice the distance gives only half a unit, which is less than one torch gave at the start.
maths.context: In the Light Meter project, you taped two torches together. Here is what happens to their light when you move them away.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the total light by the area shows why doubling the torches does not make up for doubling the distance.

quiz: Twice as far from a small lamp, the light covers four times the area.
The same light spreads over more space, so each patch gets one quarter as much.
Light is only what our eyes can see.
Infrared and ultraviolet are light our eyes cannot see, but cameras and thermometers can detect them.
When a surface absorbs light, the light's energy turns into heat.
That is why a dark tar road gets very hot in the noon sun.
Heat and light are completely different things that just travel together.
Radiant heat can be reflected and bent just like light. Both are part of one family of waves.
Plants capture sunlight, and this feeds almost all other life.
Plants turn sunlight energy into food, and animals eat plants or each other.
Light is weightless, so it cannot push anything.
Light carries a tiny push called radiation pressure. It is small but real.
Radio waves, infrared and X-rays are the same kind of wave with different wavelengths.
They are all in the light family, and they differ only in wavelength.
Radio waves cannot pass through walls.
Radio waves and microwaves pass through walls, which is how they carry phone and Wi-Fi signals.
Our skin can feel infrared as warmth, though our eyes cannot see it.
Every warm thing gives out infrared, and skin feels it as warmth.
X-rays are the longest waves in the light family.
Radio waves are the longest. X-rays are much shorter than visible light and carry a lot of energy.
odd: Radio waves, microwaves and infrared are longer than visible light. Ultraviolet is shorter.
The first three absorb much sunlight and warm up. A whitewashed wall reflects most of it.
Wi-Fi, a remote beam and phone signals belong to the light family. Sound is a different kind of wave.
Sunlight energy is never used up. It warms things, drives weather and feeds plants.
Our eyes can see red, green and violet. Infrared is beyond red, so we only feel it as warmth.
